topic.title: Trees & BST
topic.summary: Binary trees, binary search trees and tries: the four traversals, recursive “ask the children” thinking, BST search/insert/delete and the classic interview problems built on them.
topic.overview:
**Why trees matter in interviews.** Trees are the most common "real" data structure after arrays and hash maps. They test whether you can think **recursively** — solve a problem for a node by combining the answers of its subtrees — and whether you understand the difference between O(log n) and O(n) (balanced vs skewed trees). Product companies ask problems like validate BST, LCA, diameter and level order; service companies and banks often ask you to write a traversal or a BST insert on paper and explain where BSTs are used (database indexes, `TreeMap`).

**Core vocabulary**
- **Root, leaf, parent, child, subtree, depth** (distance from the root) and **height** (longest path down to a leaf).
- **Binary tree**: at most two children. **BST**: for every node, left subtree < node < right subtree.
- **Balanced** (height O(log n)), **complete** (all levels full except the last, filled left to right — the shape of a heap), **perfect** (all levels full).
- **Trie**: an n-ary tree where each edge is a character, for prefix queries.

**What you must be able to do**
1. Write **preorder, inorder, postorder** recursively and inorder **iteratively** with a stack; write **level order** with a queue.
2. Recognise the two recursion shapes: **top-down** (pass information down: bounds, depth, path so far) and **bottom-up** (return information up: height, size, "is balanced").
3. Use the **BST property** to discard half the tree per step: search, insert, delete, LCA, k-th smallest, validation.
4. State complexity precisely: **O(n)** time to visit every node, **O(h)** space for recursion, where h is between log n (balanced) and n (skewed).

**How to study**
1. Draw every example. Trace recursion on a 5–7 node tree until "trust the recursion" feels natural.
2. Learn the four templates in the patterns section by heart — almost every tree problem is one of them plus a few lines.
3. For each problem, say out loud what each call **receives** and what it **returns**.
4. Practise edge cases: empty tree, single node, skewed tree, duplicates.

cheatsheet.title: Vocabulary & facts
points: Depth = edges/nodes from the root; height = longest path down to a leaf (clarify edges vs nodes)
A tree with h levels has at most 2^h − 1 nodes; a perfect tree has about half its nodes as leaves
Height of n nodes: ⌊log₂ n⌋ (balanced) up to n − 1 (skewed, a “linked list”)
Complete tree = all levels full except the last, filled left to right (heaps use this shape)

cheatsheet.title: Traversals
points: Preorder: node, left, right — copy / serialize
Inorder: left, node, right — BST gives sorted order
Postorder: left, right, node — heights, deletion, anything needing children first
Level order: BFS with a queue; snapshot the queue size to split levels
All are O(n) time; DFS uses O(h) space, BFS O(w) (max width)

cheatsheet.title: BST operations
points: Search / insert / delete: O(h) — O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed
Delete with two children: copy the inorder successor (leftmost of right subtree), delete it from the right subtree
Validate with (low, high) bounds or a strictly increasing inorder — not a local parent/child check
Balanced BSTs in libraries: Java TreeMap/TreeSet (red-black), C++ std::map

cheatsheet.title: Recursion templates
points: Top-down: pass state into the call (bounds, depth, running sum)
Bottom-up: return a value and combine (1 + max(l, r))
“Return one thing, record another”: diameter / max path sum return one branch, record both
Two-tree recursion: symmetric, same tree, subtree — compare pairs of nodes

cheatsheet.title: Tries
points: Node = children (map or array[26]) + isEnd flag
insert / search / startsWith are O(L) for a word of length L
search needs isEnd; startsWith only needs the path
Used for autocomplete, spell check, Word Search II, longest-prefix match

cheatsheet.title: Interview checklist
points: Ask: BST or plain binary tree? Duplicates? Can it be empty? Count edges or nodes?
State O(n) time and O(h) space, and what h is for balanced vs skewed
Mention the iterative version when the tree may be very deep (stack overflow)
Dry-run on a small tree including a null child before saying you are done

questions.title: Binary Tree Traversals (Preorder, Inorder, Postorder)
questions.prompt:
Given the `root` of a binary tree (each node has `val`, `left`, `right`), return its node values in **preorder** (node → left → right), **inorder** (left → node → right) and **postorder** (left → right → node).

Then write **inorder traversal without recursion**, using an explicit stack.

examples.explanation: The tree is given in level order; null marks a missing child.
Inorder of a BST is always sorted ascending.

hints: All three orders visit the same nodes with the same recursive walk. What changes between them?
Only the moment you record `node.val` changes: before the children, between them, or after them.
For the iterative inorder, mimic the call stack: push nodes while walking left, pop one, record it, then go to its right child.

approaches.name: Recursive DFS
approaches.idea: Write a helper that recurses left and right and records the value at the right moment (pre / in / post).

approaches.name: Iterative with explicit stack
approaches.idea: Push the left path onto a stack; pop, record, then continue with the right child. Avoids stack overflow on very deep trees.

approaches.name: Morris traversal (follow-up)
approaches.idea: Temporarily link each node’s inorder predecessor back to it, so no stack is needed; the links are removed on the second visit.

solution.summary: All three are the same depth-first walk; the only difference is when I record the node: before its children (preorder), between them (inorder) or after them (postorder). Each node is visited once, so O(n) time and O(h) space for the stack, where h is the height.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** A DFS passes every node three times: on the way down, after returning from the left child, and after returning from the right child. Recording the value at each of those moments gives preorder, inorder and postorder respectively.

**Recursive version**
1. If the node is null, return.
2. *Preorder:* record the node.
3. Recurse into the left subtree.
4. *Inorder:* record the node.
5. Recurse into the right subtree.
6. *Postorder:* record the node.

**Iterative inorder** (often asked as a follow-up — "what if the tree is 100 000 levels deep?")
1. While `curr` is not null, push it and go left. The stack now holds the path to the leftmost unvisited node.
2. Pop: this is the smallest unvisited node (in a BST) — record it.
3. Move to its right child and repeat. Stop when `curr` is null **and** the stack is empty.

**Why it is correct.** A node is popped only after its entire left subtree was pushed and popped, and its right subtree is processed only after it is recorded — exactly left → node → right.

**Which one when?**
- **Preorder** — copy or serialize a tree (the root comes first, so you can rebuild it).
- **Inorder** — BSTs: sorted output, validate a BST, k-th smallest.
- **Postorder** — anything that needs the children's answers first: height, diameter, deleting/freeing a tree, evaluating an expression tree.
- **Level order** (BFS with a queue) is the fourth traversal — see the next question.

**Edge cases:** empty tree → empty lists; a skewed tree (a "linked list") makes h = n, so recursion depth is n.

code.code:
def traversals(root):
    pre, ino, post = [], [], []

    def dfs(node):
        if not node:
            return
        pre.append(node.val)   # preorder:  node, left, right
        dfs(node.left)
        ino.append(node.val)   # inorder:   left, node, right
        dfs(node.right)
        post.append(node.val)  # postorder: left, right, node

    dfs(root)
    return pre, ino, post


def inorder_iterative(root):
    out, stack = [], []
    curr = root
    while curr or stack:
        while curr:            # walk left, saving the path
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.left
        curr = stack.pop()     # leftmost unvisited node
        out.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.right      # then its right subtree
    return out

complexity.time: O(n) — every node is pushed/visited exactly once
complexity.space: O(h) — recursion or explicit stack holds one root-to-leaf path (O(n) for a skewed tree, O(log n) if balanced)

keyPoints: Pre/in/post differ only in when the value is recorded
Inorder of a BST is sorted — the basis of many BST problems
Space is O(h), not O(n): say what h is for balanced vs skewed trees
Know the iterative inorder with a stack (deep trees, no recursion)
Postorder = children first → used for height, diameter, deletion

visuals.title: One DFS, three recording moments on [1, 2, 3, null, 4]
visuals.caption: Blue = node being visited, orange = still on the call stack, light blue = fully finished. Each step appends to exactly one list.

steps.note: First visit of 1: record it **before** its children, so it goes into `preorder`.
First visit of 2: record it **before** its children, so it goes into `preorder`.
Left subtree of 2 is empty: record it **between** its children, so it goes into `inorder`.
First visit of 4: record it **before** its children, so it goes into `preorder`.
Left subtree of 4 is empty: record it **between** its children, so it goes into `inorder`.
Both subtrees of 4 are empty: record it **after** its children, so it goes into `postorder`.
Both subtrees of 2 are finished: record it **after** its children, so it goes into `postorder`.
Left subtree of 1 is finished: record it **between** its children, so it goes into `inorder`.
First visit of 3: record it **before** its children, so it goes into `preorder`.
Left subtree of 3 is empty: record it **between** its children, so it goes into `inorder`.
Both subtrees of 3 are empty: record it **after** its children, so it goes into `postorder`.
Root 1 is recorded last in `postorder`. Done: preorder [1, 2, 4, 3], inorder [2, 4, 1, 3], postorder [4, 2, 3, 1] — same walk, three different recording moments.

visuals.title: Iterative inorder with a stack on the BST [4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5]
visuals.caption: Orange = on the stack, green = already output. Notice the output comes out sorted because this is a BST.

steps.note: Start with `curr` at the root and an empty `stack`. The stack will hold the path of nodes whose left side we are still exploring.
Walk left from 4, pushing 4, 2, 1. `curr` becomes null because 1 has no left child — the top of the stack is the smallest unvisited value.
Pop 1 and append it to `out`. Then move to its right child (null), so the next pop goes back up the tree.
Pop 2 and append it to `out`. Then move to its right child (3), whose left path we explore next.
Walk left from 3, pushing 3. `curr` becomes null because 3 has no left child — the top of the stack is the smallest unvisited value.
Pop 3 and append it to `out`. Then move to its right child (null), so the next pop goes back up the tree.
Pop 4 and append it to `out`. Then move to its right child (6), whose left path we explore next.
Walk left from 6, pushing 6, 5. `curr` becomes null because 5 has no left child — the top of the stack is the smallest unvisited value.
Pop 5 and append it to `out`. Then move to its right child (null), so the next pop goes back up the tree.
Pop 6 — `curr` is null and the stack is empty, so the loop ends. On a BST, inorder gives the values **sorted**: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].

visuals.title: When to use which traversal
rows: Copy / serialize a tree, print a folder structure
BST sorted order, validate BST, k-th smallest
Height, diameter, delete a tree, evaluate expression trees
Stack: pop, record, push right then left
Stack: push left path, pop, record, go right
Two stacks, or reverse of (node → right → left)

pitfalls: Forgetting the null base case and dereferencing `node.left` of null
In the iterative version, looping only `while (stack.length)` — the stack is empty at the start and after popping the root, so the condition must be `curr || stack.length`
Saying the space is O(1) — recursion uses O(h) stack frames
Confusing level order (BFS) with preorder (DFS)

followUps.question: Can you do inorder traversal in O(1) extra space?
followUps.answer: Yes, Morris traversal: for each node with a left child, find its inorder predecessor and temporarily point the predecessor’s right pointer back to the node; remove the link on the second visit. O(n) time, O(1) space, but it mutates the tree while running.

followUps.question: Given preorder and inorder, can you rebuild the tree?
followUps.answer: Yes (with unique values): the first preorder value is the root; its position in inorder splits left and right subtrees. Use a value → index map for O(n).

followUps.question: How would you write iterative postorder?
followUps.answer: Do a modified preorder (node → right → left) with a stack, then reverse the output; or use one stack and track the last visited node.

questions.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
questions.prompt: Given the `root` of a binary tree, return its values **level by level**: a list of lists where list `d` holds the values at depth `d`, from left to right.
hints: DFS goes deep first. Which data structure visits nodes in order of their distance from the root?
A queue (FIFO): process a node, append its children to the back.
To know where one level ends, read the queue size at the start of each round and dequeue exactly that many nodes.

approaches.name: BFS with a queue + level size
approaches.idea: Snapshot `size = queue.length` at the start of each level, dequeue exactly `size` nodes, enqueue their children.
approaches.space: O(w) — w = maximum width (up to n/2)

approaches.name: DFS with depth index
approaches.idea: Recurse with `depth`; append the value to `result[depth]` (create the list the first time a depth is reached). Visiting left before right keeps each level ordered.

solution.summary: This is BFS with a queue. At the start of each round I record how many nodes are in the queue — that is exactly one level — dequeue that many, collect their values and enqueue their children. O(n) time, O(width) space.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** A queue is first-in-first-out, so nodes come out in the order they were discovered: the root, then all depth-1 nodes, then all depth-2 nodes, and so on.

**The level-size trick**
1. Start with `queue = [root]`.
2. While the queue is not empty, read `size = queue.length`. Right now the queue contains **exactly one complete level** (and nothing else).
3. Dequeue `size` nodes; add each value to `level`, enqueue its left and right children.
4. Push `level` into `result`. The queue now holds exactly the next level.

**Why it is correct.** By induction: if the queue holds exactly level d at the start of a round, then after dequeuing those `size` nodes it holds exactly their children — level d + 1 — in left-to-right order.

**Language notes.** In Python use `collections.deque` (`list.pop(0)` is O(n)); in Java use `ArrayDeque`. In JavaScript `shift()` is fine for interview-sized inputs; for very large trees keep a `head` index instead of shifting.

**This template solves a family of problems:** right side view (last of each level), zigzag order (reverse every other level), average of levels, minimum depth (first leaf found), connect next-right pointers.

complexity.time: O(n) — every node is enqueued and dequeued once
complexity.space: O(w) for the queue — the widest level, up to about n/2 in a complete tree

keyPoints: BFS = queue; DFS = stack/recursion
Snapshot the queue size to separate levels
Use a real deque (collections.deque / ArrayDeque), not list.pop(0)
Space is the maximum width, not the height
Same template: right side view, zigzag, level averages, minimum depth

visuals.title: BFS level by level on [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, null, 6, null, null, 7]
visuals.caption: Blue = node being dequeued, orange = waiting in the queue, light blue = already processed.

steps.note: Put the root in the queue. The queue always holds the next nodes to visit, in left-to-right, top-to-bottom order.
Dequeue 1 (i = 0, the last of size = 1); enqueue its children 2 and 3. The level is complete, so push [1] into `result` — the queue now holds exactly the next level.
Dequeue 2 (i = 0 of size = 2) and add it to `level`; enqueue its children 4 and 5.
Dequeue 3 (i = 1, the last of size = 2); enqueue its only child 6. The level is complete, so push [2, 3] into `result` — the queue now holds exactly the next level.
Dequeue 4 (i = 0 of size = 3) and add it to `level`; it has no children to enqueue.
Dequeue 5 (i = 1 of size = 3) and add it to `level`; enqueue its only child 7.
Dequeue 6 (i = 2, the last of size = 3); it has no children to enqueue. The level is complete, so push [4, 5, 6] into `result` — the queue now holds exactly the next level.
Dequeue 7 — the last node. The queue is empty, so the loop ends and we return [[1], [2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7]].

visuals.title: Level order with BFS vs DFS
rows: Each round of the while loop is one level
Minimum depth, right side view, shortest path in unweighted graphs
Path problems, anything needing children’s results
Good follow-up to show you know both

pitfalls: Using `queue.length` in the for-loop condition while pushing children — the length changes; snapshot it first
Using `list.pop(0)` in Python, which makes BFS O(n²)
Pushing null children into the queue and then dereferencing them
Returning `[[]]` instead of `[]` for an empty tree

followUps.question: How do you return the levels in zigzag order?
followUps.answer: Same BFS; for every odd level reverse `level` before pushing it (or insert at the front with a deque). Still O(n).

followUps.question: How do you return the levels bottom-up?
followUps.answer: Run the same BFS and reverse `result` at the end (or insert each level at the front).

followUps.question: What is the minimum depth of the tree?
followUps.answer: BFS and return the depth of the first leaf you dequeue — BFS finds it without exploring deeper levels.

questions.title: Maximum Depth of a Binary Tree
questions.prompt: Given the `root` of a binary tree, return its **maximum depth**: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. An empty tree has depth 0.

examples.explanation: Longest path: 5 → 3 → 4 → 7.

hints: If you knew the depth of the left and right subtrees, could you compute the depth of the whole tree?
depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)). What is the depth of an empty tree?
Alternatively, BFS level by level and count the levels.

approaches.name: Recursive DFS (postorder)
approaches.idea: Return 0 for null, otherwise 1 + max of the two children’s depths.

approaches.name: BFS level count
approaches.idea: Level-order traversal; increment a counter once per level.

approaches.name: Iterative DFS
approaches.idea: Stack of (node, depth) pairs; track the maximum depth seen.

solution.summary: Recursively: an empty tree has depth 0, otherwise the depth is 1 plus the larger of the two subtree depths. Every node is visited once, so O(n) time and O(h) stack space.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition — trust the recursion.** The depth of a tree depends only on the depths of its two subtrees. Solve the subproblems, then combine.

1. **Base case:** `null` → 0 (no nodes, no levels).
2. Compute `left = maxDepth(root.left)` and `right = maxDepth(root.right)`.
3. Return `1 + max(left, right)` — the current node plus the deeper side.

This is a **postorder** computation: a node's answer is ready only after both children have returned. The same "ask the children, combine, return" shape solves height-balanced check, diameter, maximum path sum and subtree sizes.

**Depth vs height:** depth is usually counted from the root, height from the leaves. Some interviewers count **edges** instead of nodes (then a single node has height 0). Ask, and adjust the base case.

**Edge cases:** empty tree (0), single node (1), a skewed tree (depth n — recursion is n frames deep; mention the iterative BFS if n can be ~10⁵).

complexity.time: O(n) — each node is visited once
complexity.space: O(h) recursion — O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed

keyPoints: Base case: null → 0
Combine: 1 + max(left, right) — a postorder computation
Clarify nodes vs edges when someone says “height”
Mention BFS level counting as the iterative alternative

visuals.title: Recursion on [5, 3, 8, null, 4, null, null, 7]
visuals.caption: Blue = current call, orange = calls waiting on the stack, light blue = returned. A returned node shows `value → depth`.

steps.note: Call maxDepth(5). Recurse into the left subtree first (3).
Call maxDepth(3). Recurse into the left subtree first — it is null, so it returns 0 immediately.
Call maxDepth(4). Recurse into the left subtree first (7).
Call maxDepth(7). It is a leaf: both recursive calls hit null and return 0.
maxDepth(7) returns 1 + max(left = 0, right = 0) = **1**. Its parent will use this value.
maxDepth(4) returns 1 + max(left = 1, right = 0) = **2**. Its parent will use this value.
maxDepth(3) returns 1 + max(left = 0, right = 2) = **3**. Its parent will use this value.
Call maxDepth(8). It is a leaf: both recursive calls hit null and return 0.
maxDepth(8) returns 1 + max(left = 0, right = 0) = **1**. Its parent will use this value.
The root returns 1 + max(3, 1) = **4**: the longest root-to-leaf path is 5 → 3 → 4 → 7.

rows: Count rounds of the level loop
Stack of (node, depth); keep the max
Stack overflow on very deep (skewed) trees
Large queue on very wide trees

pitfalls: Returning 1 for a null node (off by one everywhere)
Taking `min` instead of `max`, or adding depths of both sides (that is the diameter idea)
Mixing up node-count depth with edge-count height without saying which one you use

followUps.question: What is the minimum depth?
followUps.answer: Careful: a node with one child is not a leaf. Use BFS and return at the first leaf, or recursively use the non-null child when one side is null.

followUps.question: How do you check if a tree is height-balanced?
followUps.answer: Postorder: return the height, or -1 if any subtree is unbalanced or |hL − hR| > 1. One pass, O(n).

questions.title: Invert (Mirror) a Binary Tree
questions.prompt: Given the `root` of a binary tree, **mirror** it in place — swap the left and right child of every node — and return the root.
hints: What is the inverse of a single node with two leaf children?
If both subtrees were already inverted, what is left to do at the root?
Swap the children of the current node, then invert both subtrees recursively (any traversal order works as long as every node is visited once).

approaches.name: Recursive DFS
approaches.idea: Swap children, recurse into both subtrees. Preorder or postorder both work.

approaches.name: Iterative BFS
approaches.idea: Queue of nodes; pop one, swap its children, enqueue the non-null children.

solution.summary: Visit every node once and swap its left and right pointers; recursing into both children mirrors the whole tree. O(n) time and O(h) space for the recursion.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** A mirror image swaps left and right at **every** level, not just at the root. So the job at each node is tiny — swap two pointers — and recursion applies it everywhere.

1. If `root` is null, return null.
2. Swap `root.left` and `root.right` (use a temporary variable, or tuple assignment in Python).
3. Recursively invert the (new) left and right subtrees.
4. Return `root`.

**Order does not matter** as long as each node is swapped exactly once: preorder (swap, then recurse) and postorder (recurse, then swap) both work. Inorder is the trap — recurse left, swap, recurse right: after the swap, `root.right` is the subtree you already inverted, so it gets inverted back, and the original right subtree is never inverted at all.

**Iterative version:** BFS with a queue — pop a node, swap its children, push the non-null children. Useful if the tree may be too deep for recursion.

**Edge cases:** empty tree, single node, skewed tree (becomes skewed the other way).

code.code:
def invert_tree(root):
    if not root:
        return None
    root.left, root.right = root.right, root.left  # swap the two children
    invert_tree(root.left)                         # then mirror each subtree
    invert_tree(root.right)
    return root

complexity.space: O(h) recursion (O(w) for the BFS version)

keyPoints: Swap at every node, not only at the root
Preorder or postorder both work; inorder swaps one subtree twice
In-place: no new nodes are created
Offer the BFS version for very deep trees

visuals.title: Preorder swapping on [5, 3, 8, 1, 4, 7, 9]
visuals.caption: Blue = node whose children were just swapped, light blue = already mirrored. Watch whole subtrees move with each swap.

steps.note: The original tree. Inverting means every node’s left and right children trade places — a mirror image.
invertTree(5): swap its children (3, 8) → (8, 3). Then recurse into the new left child 8.
invertTree(8): swap its children (7, 9) → (9, 7). Then recurse into the new left child 9.
invertTree(9): a leaf — swapping two nulls changes nothing, and both recursive calls return immediately.
invertTree(7): a leaf — swapping two nulls changes nothing, and both recursive calls return immediately.
invertTree(3): swap its children (1, 4) → (4, 1). Then recurse into the new left child 4.
invertTree(4): a leaf — swapping two nulls changes nothing, and both recursive calls return immediately.
invertTree(1): a leaf — swapping two nulls changes nothing, and both recursive calls return immediately.
Every call has returned; the original root is returned. Reading the levels now gives [5, 8, 3, 9, 7, 4, 1] — the mirror image.

pitfalls: Overwriting `root.left` before saving it, losing the left subtree
Using inorder (recurse left, swap, recurse right): after the swap, `root.right` is the subtree you already inverted, so it is inverted back and the original right subtree is never touched
Building a new tree when an in-place swap was asked for (fine if asked, but say so)

followUps.question: How would you check that one tree is the mirror of another?
followUps.answer: Compare pairs: roots equal, a.left mirrors b.right and a.right mirrors b.left — the same recursion as Symmetric Tree.

followUps.question: Can you do it without recursion?
followUps.answer: Yes, BFS or DFS with an explicit queue/stack: pop a node, swap its children, push the non-null children.

questions.title: Symmetric Tree
questions.prompt: Given the `root` of a binary tree, return `true` if the tree is a **mirror image of itself** around its center (the left subtree is the reflection of the right subtree), otherwise `false`. Both values and shape must match.

examples.explanation: Values match per level, but both 3s are right children, so the shape is not mirrored.

hints: Comparing one tree with itself is hard; compare two subtrees with each other instead.
Two trees a and b are mirrors when their roots are equal and a.left mirrors b.right, a.right mirrors b.left.
Handle the null cases first: both null → true, exactly one null → false.

approaches.name: Level lists + palindrome check
approaches.idea: BFS each level including nulls and check every level reads the same both ways. Works but builds lists and must include null placeholders.

approaches.name: Recursive pairwise mirror check
approaches.idea: isMirror(a, b): equal values, isMirror(a.left, b.right) and isMirror(a.right, b.left).

approaches.name: Iterative with a queue of pairs
approaches.idea: Push (left, right); pop a pair, compare, push (a.left, b.right) and (a.right, b.left).

solution.summary: I compare the left and right subtrees as a pair: they are mirrors when both are null, or both exist with equal values and the outer children (a.left, b.right) and inner children (a.right, b.left) are mirrors too. Each node is compared once: O(n) time, O(h) space.
solution.explanation:
**Reframe.** "Is this tree symmetric?" = "Is the left subtree a mirror of the right subtree?" — a question about **two** trees, which recursion handles naturally.

**isMirror(a, b)**
1. Both null → `true` (empty mirrors empty).
2. Exactly one null → `false` (the shapes differ).
3. Otherwise require `a.val === b.val` **and** `isMirror(a.left, b.right)` (outer pair) **and** `isMirror(a.right, b.left)` (inner pair).

The answer is `isMirror(root.left, root.right)`.

**Why both checks matter.** The second example has the same values on every level, so a values-only check passes; the structure check (null vs non-null) is what catches it.

**Short-circuiting.** `&&` stops at the first mismatch, so an asymmetric tree is often rejected early.

**Edge cases:** empty tree and single node are symmetric; duplicates are fine because we compare positions, not sets of values.

complexity.time: O(n) — every node takes part in at most one comparison

keyPoints: Turn one-tree symmetry into a two-tree mirror check
Outer pair (a.left, b.right) and inner pair (a.right, b.left)
Null handling first: both null → true, one null → false
Shape matters, not just values per level

visuals.title: Symmetric: [1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 3]
visuals.caption: Blue = the pair (a, b) being compared, green = pairs whose values already matched (all green at the end = every pair mirrored).

steps.note: A tree is symmetric if its left subtree is the mirror image of its right subtree. Start with the pair (root.left, root.right).
Compare the top pair: a.val = 2 equals b.val = 2. Next check the outer pair (a.left, b.right), then the inner pair (a.right, b.left).
Compare the outer pair: a.val = 3 equals b.val = 3. Both are leaves, so the outer and inner calls are isMirror(null, null) → true.
Compare the inner pair: a.val = 4 equals b.val = 4. Both are leaves, so the outer and inner calls are isMirror(null, null) → true.
Every mirrored pair matched and every null lined up with a null, so `isSymmetric` returns **true**.

visuals.title: Not symmetric: [1, 2, 2, null, 3, null, 3]
visuals.caption: Same values per level, different shape. Red = the node whose mirror partner is missing.

steps.note: A tree is symmetric if its left subtree is the mirror image of its right subtree. Start with the pair (root.left, root.right).
Compare the top pair: a.val = 2 equals b.val = 2. Next check the outer pair (a.left, b.right), then the inner pair (a.right, b.left).
Check the outer pair: one side is **null** but the other is 3. The shapes differ, so isMirror returns **false** — and `&&` short-circuits all the way up.
The values match level by level ([2, 2] and [3, 3]), but the **shape** is not mirrored: both 3s hang on the right. `isSymmetric` returns **false**.

pitfalls: Comparing a.left with b.left (that checks equality, not mirroring)
Only comparing values level by level and ignoring null positions
Dereferencing a null child before the null checks

followUps.question: Can you solve it iteratively?
followUps.answer: Use a queue of pairs: start with (root.left, root.right); pop a pair, apply the same three checks, then push (a.left, b.right) and (a.right, b.left).

followUps.question: How do you check if two trees are identical?
followUps.answer: Same recursion but compare a.left with b.left and a.right with b.right.

questions.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
questions.prompt:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return `true` if it is a valid **binary search tree**:
- every value in a node's **left subtree** is strictly smaller than the node's value,
- every value in its **right subtree** is strictly greater,
- and both subtrees are themselves BSTs.

examples.explanation: 9 is in the left subtree of 8 but 9 > 8 — even though 9 > 4 locally.
Duplicates are not allowed (strict inequality).

hints: Checking only node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val is not enough. Why?
Every node has a range of allowed values decided by all its ancestors, not just its parent.
Pass (low, high) down: going left tightens high to node.val, going right tightens low to node.val. Alternatively, an inorder traversal must be strictly increasing.

approaches.name: Local parent/child check (wrong)
approaches.idea: Only compare each node with its direct children. Accepts [8, 4, 12, 2, 9] — a classic interview trap.

approaches.name: Subtree min/max for every node
approaches.idea: For each node compute the max of the left subtree and min of the right subtree separately.

approaches.name: DFS with (low, high) bounds
approaches.idea: Each node must lie strictly inside the window inherited from its ancestors.

approaches.name: Inorder must be strictly increasing
approaches.idea: Inorder traversal of a BST is sorted; compare each value with the previous one.

solution.summary: Every node must fall inside a (low, high) range set by its ancestors. I recurse with that window: going left the upper bound becomes the node’s value, going right the lower bound does. Any node outside its window means it is not a BST. O(n) time, O(h) space.
solution.explanation:
**The trap.** The BST property is about **whole subtrees**, not just children. In `[8, 4, 12, 2, 9]`, node 9 is a fine right child of 4, but it lives in 8's left subtree, so it must be < 8.

**Bounds approach**
1. Call `isValidBST(root, -∞, +∞)`.
2. At a node, if `val <= low` or `val >= high`, return false (strict, so duplicates are rejected).
3. Recurse left with `(low, val)` — everything on the left must be smaller than this node.
4. Recurse right with `(val, high)` — everything on the right must be larger.
5. Empty subtrees are valid.

**Why it is correct.** The window at a node is exactly the intersection of the constraints from all its ancestors: each time we go left past an ancestor we learn "< that ancestor", each time we go right we learn "> that ancestor".

**Alternative — inorder.** An iterative inorder traversal visits a BST in strictly increasing order; keep `prev` and fail if `curr.val <= prev`. Same complexity and a nice follow-up to mention.

**Edge cases.** Values at the integer limits: in Java, `Integer.MIN_VALUE` as a sentinel breaks for a node with that value — use `long` bounds or nullable `Integer`. Ask whether duplicates are allowed (here: no).

complexity.time: O(n) — each node is checked once

keyPoints: Explain why the local parent/child check fails, with an example
Carry (low, high) bounds from ancestors; tighten one bound per step
Strict inequalities — clarify duplicates with the interviewer
Mention the inorder-is-strictly-increasing alternative
Java: use long or null bounds to handle Integer.MIN_VALUE / MAX_VALUE

visuals.title: Bounds check on the trap tree [8, 4, 12, 2, 9, 10, 14]
visuals.caption: Each visited node shows `value (low,high)`: its allowed window. Green = inside the window, red = violation, grey = never visited.

steps.note: Every node passes the **local** check (left child < parent < right child): 9 > 4 as 4’s right child. Yet 9 sits in the **left** subtree of 8, so this is not a BST. Each node must respect bounds from all its ancestors.
Visit 8 with allowed range (-∞, ∞): inside, OK. Its left child gets (-∞, 8) and its right child gets (8, ∞).
Visit 4 with allowed range (-∞, 8): inside, OK. Its left child gets (-∞, 4) and its right child gets (4, 8).
Visit 2 with allowed range (-∞, 4): inside, OK. Its left child gets (-∞, 2) and its right child gets (2, 4).
Visit 9 with allowed range (4, 8). 9 ≥ high = 8 — it is bigger than its ancestor 8 although it lives in 8’s left subtree. Return **false**.
`false` propagates up through the `&&` chain; the right subtree of 8 is never even visited. A correct BST check must carry the (low, high) window down from the ancestors.

visuals.title: Approaches to validating a BST
rows: Compare with the previous inorder value

pitfalls: Only comparing a node with its direct children
Using <= / >= inconsistently and accepting duplicates
Using Integer.MIN_VALUE / MAX_VALUE as sentinels in Java and failing for nodes with those values
Collecting the full inorder list when a running `prev` value is enough

followUps.question: How would you do it with an inorder traversal?
followUps.answer: Iterative inorder with a stack, keeping `prev`. If any value is <= prev, return false. O(n) time, O(h) space.

followUps.question: Two nodes of a BST were swapped by mistake. How do you fix it?
followUps.answer: Inorder traversal finds the two places where the order drops (first violation’s larger value, last violation’s smaller value); swap those two values back. O(n), and O(1) space with Morris traversal.

questions.title: Lowest Common Ancestor in a BST
questions.prompt: Given the `root` of a **binary search tree** and two nodes `p` and `q` that are both in the tree, return their **lowest common ancestor (LCA)**: the deepest node that has both `p` and `q` as descendants. A node counts as a descendant of itself.

examples.explanation: p is an ancestor of q, and a node is a descendant of itself.

constraints: p ≠ q and both exist in the tree
hints: Use the BST ordering: from a node, can you tell which subtree p and q are in without searching?
If both values are smaller than the node, the LCA is in the left subtree; if both are larger, in the right subtree.
The first node where they are not on the same side (or where node equals p or q) is the answer.

approaches.name: Generic binary-tree LCA
approaches.idea: Recursive DFS that returns a node if p or q is found in its subtree. Ignores the BST order.

approaches.name: Store both root paths
approaches.idea: Search p and q from the root, record both paths, return the last common node.

approaches.name: Walk down from the root (BST)
approaches.idea: Move left while both are smaller, right while both are larger; stop at the split.

solution.summary: Start at the root: if both values are smaller go left, if both are larger go right; otherwise p and q split here (or one of them is this node), so this node is the LCA. That is one root-to-node walk: O(h) time and O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** In a BST, the value of a node tells you which subtree any other value would be in. Walking down from the root, p and q follow the same path until the first node where they go different ways — that node is their lowest common ancestor.

1. `node = root`.
2. If `p.val` and `q.val` are both less than `node.val`, the LCA is in the left subtree: `node = node.left`.
3. If both are greater, `node = node.right`.
4. Otherwise one is ≤ node and the other ≥ node: **return node**. This also covers `node === p` or `node === q` (an ancestor of itself).

**Why it is correct.** Every node above the split point is a common ancestor (both are below it, on the same side). At the split, going left loses q and going right loses p, so no deeper node can contain both.

**Complexity.** One path from the root: O(h) — O(log n) for a balanced BST, O(n) for a degenerate one. The loop uses O(1) space (the recursive version uses O(h) stack).

**If the tree is not a BST** you cannot steer by value; use the general recursive LCA (see follow-ups).

complexity.time: O(h) — one walk from the root toward the split point

keyPoints: Exploit the BST ordering — no need to search both subtrees
Split point = first node where p and q go different ways
A node is a descendant of itself (p can be the answer)
O(h): say what h is for balanced vs skewed BSTs
Know the general binary-tree LCA as the follow-up

visuals.title: LCA of 12 and 18 in [20, 10, 30, 5, 15, 25, 35, null, null, 12, 18]
visuals.caption: Orange = p and q, blue = current node, light blue = path so far, grey = subtrees skipped thanks to the BST order.

steps.note: Find the lowest common ancestor of p = 12 and q = 18. In a BST we never need to search both subtrees: comparing with the current value tells us which side both nodes are on.
node = 20: both 12 and 18 are smaller, so both live in the left subtree — move left. The whole right subtree is skipped.
node = 10: both 12 and 18 are larger, so both live in the right subtree — move right. The left subtree (5 and below) is skipped.
node = 15: 12 < 15 < 18, so p and q are on **different sides** — this is where their paths from the root split. Return 15.

visuals.title: LCA in a BST vs in a general binary tree
rows: Value ordering to pick a side
Loop: left if both smaller, right if both larger, else stop
Recursive: if node is p or q return it; combine left/right results; if both non-null, node is the LCA

pitfalls: Searching both subtrees as if it were a plain binary tree (correct but misses the point)
Forgetting the case where p is an ancestor of q
Comparing node references with values, or using p.val > node.val || q.val > node.val (wrong logic)

followUps.question: How do you find the LCA in a general binary tree?
followUps.answer: Recursive DFS: return null for null, return node if it is p or q; recurse left and right; if both results are non-null, the current node is the LCA, otherwise return the non-null one. O(n) time.

followUps.question: What if p or q might not be in the tree?
followUps.answer: First verify both exist (two BST searches, O(h)), or have the DFS count how many targets it found and only accept the answer if the count is 2.

questions.title: BST Search, Insert and Delete
questions.prompt:
Implement the three core operations of a **binary search tree** with unique integer values:

- `searchBST(root, key)` — return the node holding `key`, or `null`.
- `insertIntoBST(root, key)` — insert `key` (not already present) and return the root.
- `deleteNode(root, key)` — remove `key` if present and return the (possibly new) root. The result must still be a valid BST.

examples.input: root = [50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, null, null, null, null, 55, 65], deleteNode(root, 50)
examples.explanation: 50 has two children: copy its successor 55 up, then delete the old 55 leaf.
Key not present.

constraints: Target O(h) per operation, where h is the tree height
hints: Search and insert follow one path: compare, then go to the only side where the key can be.
For delete, split into cases by how many children the node has. Leaves and single-child nodes are easy — what replaces them?
With two children, replace the value with the inorder successor (smallest in the right subtree), then delete that successor from the right subtree; it has at most one child.

approaches.name: Rebuild from a sorted list
approaches.idea: Inorder → remove/add the key → rebuild a balanced BST. Correct but O(n) per operation.

approaches.name: Recursive BST operations
approaches.idea: Walk one path; for delete handle 0 / 1 / 2 children, using the inorder successor for 2.

solution.summary: Search and insert walk one path down using the BST order. Delete finds the node, then: a leaf or single-child node is replaced by its child; a node with two children takes the value of its inorder successor (leftmost node of its right subtree), and that successor is deleted from the right subtree. All O(h).
solution.explanation:
**Search.** Compare `key` with the node: equal → found; smaller → go left; larger → go right. Each step discards a whole subtree.

**Insert.** Search for the key; the null pointer where the search falls off is exactly where the new leaf belongs. The recursive version returns the subtree root so the parent can re-link: `root.left = insertIntoBST(root.left, key)`.

**Delete — three cases**
1. **Leaf (0 children):** return `null` — the parent's pointer is cleared.
2. **One child:** return that child — it takes the node's place (the order still holds because the whole subtree was on the correct side of the parent).
3. **Two children:** find the **inorder successor** — go right once, then left as far as possible. Copy its value into the node, then delete the successor from the right subtree. The successor has no left child, so that second delete is case 1 or 2.

Using the **inorder predecessor** (rightmost node of the left subtree) works just as well.

**Why the two-children case keeps the BST valid.** The successor is the smallest value larger than the deleted key: it is larger than everything in the left subtree and no larger than anything left in the right subtree.

**Complexity.** O(h) for all three: O(log n) when balanced, O(n) for a degenerate tree (e.g. inserting sorted data). That is why production code uses **self-balancing** trees — Java's `TreeMap` is a red-black tree.

complexity.time: O(h) per operation — one root-to-leaf path (O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed)
complexity.space: O(h) for the recursion (search is O(1) iterative)

keyPoints: Search/insert follow a single path — O(h)
Delete: 0 children → null, 1 child → that child, 2 children → successor
Successor = leftmost node in the right subtree (or use the predecessor)
Return the subtree root from recursive calls so parents re-link correctly
Unbalanced BSTs degrade to O(n); mention AVL / red-black trees (TreeMap)

visuals.title: Delete 50 (two children) from [50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, null, null, null, null, 55, 65]
visuals.caption: Red = node being removed, orange = successor candidate, light blue = path walked, green = node that received the successor value.

steps.note: Delete key = 50 — the root, which has **two** children. We cannot just remove it; we replace its value with the next larger value (the inorder successor) and delete that node instead.
Found it (key === root.val). Both children exist, so start the successor search at the right child: `succ = root.right` (70).
succ has a left child, so go left to 60. The successor is the **leftmost** (smallest) node of the right subtree.
succ has a left child, so go left to 55. The successor is the **leftmost** (smallest) node of the right subtree. It has no left child, so 55 is the successor.
Copy the successor's value into the root: root.val = 55. Every value on the left (< 50) is still smaller and every value on the right is ≥ 55, so the order holds — but 55 now appears twice.
deleteNode(70, 55): 55 < 70, recurse left.
deleteNode(60, 55): 55 < 60, recurse left.
deleteNode(55, 55): found the old copy. It has no left child, so return its right child (null) — the parent's pointer skips over it.
The duplicate 55 is gone; the calls return up the path and the root (now 55) is returned. The result is still a valid BST: inorder is [20, 30, 40, 55, 60, 65, 70, 80].

visuals.title: Insert 45 into the same BST
visuals.caption: Light blue = path compared, green = the new leaf.

steps.note: Insert key = 45. Like a search, each comparison rules out one whole subtree; the new value always ends up as a **leaf**.
45 < 50, so recurse into the left subtree (30).
45 > 30, so recurse into the right subtree (40).
45 > 40, so recurse into the right subtree, which is **null**.
insertIntoBST(null, 45) creates a new node; the caller stores it with `root.right = ...`, attaching 45 as the right child of 40.
Each call returns its (unchanged) root back up the path, so the original root is returned. Cost: one root-to-leaf path, O(h).

visuals.title: The three delete cases
rows: Return null — the parent forgets it
Return the only child — it moves up one level
Copy the inorder successor’s value, then delete the successor from the right subtree
Delete 50 → root becomes 55, old 55 leaf removed
Reach null and return null — nothing changes

pitfalls: Forgetting to assign the recursive result back (`root.left = deleteNode(...)`), so the deletion never reaches the parent
For two children, taking the right child itself instead of the leftmost node of the right subtree
Deleting the successor by value from the whole tree (root) instead of from the right subtree
Claiming O(log n) without saying “if the tree is balanced”

followUps.question: Why do real libraries use balanced BSTs?
followUps.answer: Inserting sorted keys into a plain BST builds a linked list, so operations become O(n). AVL and red-black trees rotate after inserts/deletes to keep the height O(log n); Java TreeMap/TreeSet and C++ std::map are red-black trees.

followUps.question: How would you find the inorder successor of a node without a parent pointer?
followUps.answer: If it has a right child: leftmost node of the right subtree. Otherwise walk from the root: every time you go left, remember that node as a candidate; the last candidate is the successor. O(h).

questions.title: Diameter of a Binary Tree
questions.pattern: Tree DFS returning height + global answer
questions.prompt: Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the length of its **diameter**: the number of **edges** on the longest path between any two nodes. The path does not have to pass through the root.

examples.input: root = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, null, null, 6, null, null, 7, 8, null, null, 9]
examples.explanation: Path 8 → 6 → 4 → 2 → 5 → 7 → 9 bends at node 2, not at the root.
For example 4 → 2 → 1 → 3.

hints: Any path has a single highest node where it turns from going up to going down. What is the longest path that turns at a given node?
It is height(left subtree) + height(right subtree), measured in edges from that node.
Compute heights bottom-up with one DFS, and update a global maximum of left + right at every node.

approaches.name: Height from scratch at every node
approaches.idea: For each node call a separate height() on both children and take the max of left + right over all nodes.

approaches.name: Single postorder DFS
approaches.idea: height() returns the subtree height and, as a side effect, updates best = max(best, left + right).

solution.summary: One postorder DFS: each call returns the height of its subtree, and at every node I update a global best with left height + right height, which is the longest path bending at that node. The answer is the best seen. O(n) time, O(h) space.
solution.explanation:
**Key observation.** Every path has a highest node (its "bend"). The longest path bending at node X goes down X's left subtree as deep as possible and down its right subtree as deep as possible: **height(left) + height(right)** edges (with height counted in nodes, the null child has height 0).

**Algorithm**
1. `height(null) = 0`.
2. For a node, get `left = height(node.left)` and `right = height(node.right)`.
3. Update `best = max(best, left + right)` — the candidate path bending here.
4. Return `1 + max(left, right)` to the parent — a parent can only extend **one** side of this node's path.

**The crucial distinction:** what you *return* (height, one branch) is different from what you *record* (left + right, both branches). Mixing them up is the most common bug.

**Why not just height(root.left) + height(root.right)?** The longest path may not pass through the root — in the example the root offers only 5 edges while node 2 offers 6.

**Edges vs nodes:** this counts edges. If the interviewer wants nodes, return `best + 1`.

code.code:
def diameter_of_binary_tree(root):
    best = 0                               # longest path seen, in edges

    def height(node):
        nonlocal best
        if not node:
            return 0
        left = height(node.left)
        right = height(node.right)
        best = max(best, left + right)     # longest path that bends at node
        return 1 + max(left, right)        # height of this subtree

    height(root)
    return best

complexity.time: O(n) — each node is visited once

keyPoints: Every path bends at exactly one highest node
Record left + right, but return 1 + max(left, right)
The diameter need not pass through the root
Same pattern: maximum path sum, longest univalue path, balanced-tree check

visuals.title: Postorder heights on [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, null, null, 6, null, null, 7, 8, null, null, 9]
visuals.caption: Returned nodes show `value (h=height)`. Blue = node returning now, green = the best path found so far.

steps.note: Every path has one highest node where it "bends". If we know the heights of a node’s two subtrees, the longest path bending there has left + right edges. A postorder DFS computes all heights in one pass.
height(8): left = 0, right = 0. A path bending here has 0 + 0 = 0 edges (best stays 0). Return height 1 + max = 1.
height(6): left = 1, right = 0. A path bending here has 1 + 0 = 1 edge — a new best, **best = 1**. Return height 1 + max = 2.
height(4): left = 2, right = 0. A path bending here has 2 + 0 = 2 edges — a new best, **best = 2**. Return height 1 + max = 3.
height(9): left = 0, right = 0. A path bending here has 0 + 0 = 0 edges (best stays 2). Return height 1 + max = 1.
height(7): left = 0, right = 1. A path bending here has 0 + 1 = 1 edge (best stays 2). Return height 1 + max = 2.
height(5): left = 0, right = 2. A path bending here has 0 + 2 = 2 edges (best stays 2). Return height 1 + max = 3.
height(2): left = 3, right = 3. A path bending here has 3 + 3 = 6 edges — a new best, **best = 6**. Return height 1 + max = 4.
height(3): left = 0, right = 0. A path bending here has 0 + 0 = 0 edges (best stays 6). Return height 1 + max = 1.
height(1): left = 4, right = 1. A path bending here has 4 + 1 = 5 edges (best stays 6). Return height 1 + max = 5.
Done: the diameter is **6 edges** (8 → 6 → 4 → 2 → 5 → 7 → 9). It bends at node 2 and does **not** pass through the root — the root only offers 4 + 1 = 5.

visuals.title: Naive vs single-pass diameter
rows: Two full height() calls over its subtrees
Max path sum, balanced check, longest univalue path

pitfalls: Returning left + right to the parent instead of 1 + max(left, right)
Only checking the path through the root
Counting nodes instead of edges (off by one) without saying so
In Java/Python forgetting to reset the global `best` between calls (field / nonlocal)

followUps.question: How would you solve Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum?
followUps.answer: Same shape: gain(node) = node.val + max(0, gain(left), gain(right)) is returned; record node.val + max(0, gainL) + max(0, gainR) as a candidate. Negative branches are dropped with max(0, …).

followUps.question: What if the tree is a general graph (no root)?
followUps.answer: For a tree as an undirected graph: BFS from any node to find the farthest node A, then BFS from A; the farthest distance is the diameter.

questions.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
questions.prompt: Given the `root` of a **binary search tree** and an integer `k` (1-indexed), return the **k-th smallest** value in the tree.
hints: Which traversal of a BST produces the values in sorted order?
You do not need the whole sorted list — only the first k values.
Use an iterative inorder with a stack and return as soon as you have popped k nodes.

approaches.name: Collect all + sort
approaches.idea: Traverse in any order, sort the values, take index k − 1. Ignores the BST property.

approaches.name: Full inorder list
approaches.idea: Inorder gives sorted order directly; return list[k − 1].

approaches.name: Iterative inorder, stop at k
approaches.idea: Stack-based inorder; count pops and return at the k-th.

solution.summary: Inorder traversal visits a BST in ascending order, so I run an iterative inorder with a stack and return the k-th node I pop. It stops early, so it costs O(h + k) time and O(h) space.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** For a BST, **inorder = sorted**. The k-th smallest is simply the k-th node an inorder traversal visits.

**Iterative inorder with early exit**
1. Push nodes while walking left from `curr`; the top of the stack is the smallest unvisited value.
2. Pop a node and decrement `k`. If `k` hits 0, return its value.
3. Move to its right child and repeat.

**Why iterative?** The recursive version needs extra plumbing (a counter outside the recursion plus a way to stop early). The stack version can simply `return` the moment it has the answer.

**Complexity.** We descend at most h levels before the first pop and then pop k nodes, so **O(h + k)** — much better than O(n) when k is small. Space is the stack, O(h).

**Edge cases.** k = 1 is the leftmost node; k = n is the rightmost; a skewed tree makes h = n.

code.code:
def kth_smallest(root, k):
    stack, curr = [], root
    while curr or stack:
        while curr:                  # go as far left as possible
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.left
        curr = stack.pop()           # next smallest value
        k -= 1
        if k == 0:
            return curr.val          # the k-th one popped
        curr = curr.right
    return -1                        # k is larger than the tree

complexity.time: O(h + k) — descend once, then pop k nodes
complexity.space: O(h) — the stack holds one path

keyPoints: Inorder of a BST is sorted ascending
Stop as soon as the k-th node is popped — O(h + k), not O(n)
Iterative stack makes the early exit trivial
Frequent queries with updates → store subtree sizes in each node (order-statistic tree) for O(h) per query

visuals.title: k = 3 on the BST [5, 3, 7, 2, 4, 6, 8, 1]
visuals.caption: Orange = on the stack, blue = just popped, green = popped earlier (ascending order); the last step marks the answer green and the earlier pops light blue. Grey = never reached thanks to the early exit.

steps.note: Inorder traversal of a BST visits values in ascending order, so the k-th node we pop is the k-th smallest. Start with k = 3 and `curr` at the root.
Walk left pushing 5, 3, 2, 1. The top of the stack (1) is now the smallest value not yet visited.
Pop 1 — the 1st smallest — so k drops to 2. Continue with its right child (null).
Pop 2 — the 2nd smallest — so k drops to 1. Continue with its right child (null).
Pop 3: k becomes 0, so 3 is the 3rd smallest — return it **immediately**. Node 5 is still waiting on the stack and is never popped; 4, 7, 6 and 8 are never even reached.

visuals.title: Approaches for the k-th smallest
rows: One query, small k — the expected answer
Many queries while the tree changes

pitfalls: Collecting the whole inorder list when an early exit is possible
Off-by-one: k is 1-indexed (return list[k − 1] if you do use a list)
Recursive version that keeps traversing after the answer is found

followUps.question: What if the BST is modified often and you query k-th smallest often?
followUps.answer: Augment each node with the size of its subtree. At a node, if size(left) ≥ k go left; if size(left) + 1 = k return the node; else go right with k − size(left) − 1. O(h) per query, and sizes are updated on insert/delete.

followUps.question: How do you find the k-th largest?
followUps.answer: Reverse inorder (right → node → left), or the (n − k + 1)-th smallest.

questions.title: Binary Tree Right Side View
questions.prompt: Imagine standing to the **right** of a binary tree. Return the values of the nodes you can see, ordered from top to bottom — that is, the **rightmost node of each level**.

examples.explanation: 7 is in the left subtree, but nothing on the right side reaches that depth.

hints: Following right pointers from the root is not enough. Why?
You need exactly one node per depth: the rightmost one at that depth.
Level-order traversal: the last node dequeued on each level is visible. Or DFS visiting right before left, recording the first node seen at each new depth.

approaches.name: Follow right pointers (wrong)
approaches.idea: Walk root → right → right… Misses deeper levels that only exist in the left subtree.

approaches.name: BFS, last node per level
approaches.idea: Level-order traversal with the size trick; record the node at i = size − 1.

approaches.name: DFS right-first
approaches.idea: Preorder visiting right before left; when depth === view.length this is the first (rightmost) node at that depth.

solution.summary: The visible nodes are the last node of each level, so I do a level-order BFS and, on every level, record the node at index size − 1. Every node is processed once: O(n) time, O(width) space.
solution.explanation:
**The trap.** "Right side" does not mean "right children". If the right subtree is shorter, deeper levels are visible through the left subtree (node 7 in the example).

**BFS solution**
1. Queue the root.
2. For each level, snapshot `size = queue.length` and dequeue `size` nodes.
3. The node with `i === size - 1` is the rightmost on that level — append it to `view`.
4. Enqueue children left then right so the order within the next level stays left-to-right.

**DFS alternative (O(h) space).** Recurse with `depth`, visiting the **right child first**. The first node you reach at each depth is the rightmost one: `if (depth === view.length) view.push(node.val)`.

**Variations:** left side view (record `i === 0`, or DFS left-first), bottom view / top view (need horizontal distance), largest value per level.

complexity.time: O(n) — each node is enqueued and dequeued once
complexity.space: O(w) — the widest level sits in the queue

keyPoints: Visible node = last node of each level, not “the right child”
BFS with the level-size snapshot; record i === size − 1
DFS right-first with depth === result.length is the O(h)-space alternative
Left side view is the mirror: first node per level

visuals.title: BFS right side view of [1, 2, 3, null, 5, null, 4, 7]
visuals.caption: Green = visible (last on its level), grey = hidden, orange = waiting in the queue.

steps.note: Standing on the right, you see the **last** node of every level — not necessarily a right child. BFS level by level and keep the last node of each level.
Level 0: 1 is the only node on this level, so it is visible — append 1 to `view`.
Level 1: dequeue 2 (i = 0, size = 2). It is hidden behind a node further right on the same level.
Level 1: 3 is the last of the 2 nodes on this level (i = 1 = size − 1), so it is visible — append 3 to `view`.
Level 2: dequeue 5 (i = 0, size = 2). It is hidden behind a node further right on the same level.
Level 2: 4 is the last of the 2 nodes on this level (i = 1 = size − 1), so it is visible — append 4 to `view`.
Level 3: 7 is the only node on this level, so it is visible — append 7 to `view`. Note 7 is in the **left** subtree: the right subtree simply has nothing that deep.
The queue is empty. The right side view is [1, 3, 4, 7].

visuals.title: BFS vs DFS for the right side view

pitfalls: Only following right pointers and missing deeper left-subtree levels
Using the live queue length inside the level loop instead of a snapshot
In the DFS version, visiting left before right (gives the left side view)

followUps.question: How do you get the left side view?
followUps.answer: Record the node at i === 0 in BFS, or do DFS visiting the left child first.

followUps.question: How would you compute the bottom view?
followUps.answer: BFS while tracking each node’s horizontal distance (root 0, left −1, right +1); the last node seen for each distance is visible from below. Sort by distance at the end.

questions.title: Implement a Trie (Prefix Tree)
questions.prompt:
Implement a **trie** (prefix tree) for lowercase English words with three operations:

- `insert(word)` — add `word` to the trie.
- `search(word)` — return `true` if `word` was inserted before.
- `startsWith(prefix)` — return `true` if any inserted word starts with `prefix`.

examples.explanation: "ca" is a prefix, not an inserted word.

hints: Words that share a prefix should share storage. What tree shape does that suggest?
Each node maps a character to a child node. A path from the root spells a prefix.
You also need a flag on each node saying whether a complete word ends there — otherwise "car" and "card" are indistinguishable from "ca".

approaches.name: List of words
approaches.idea: Store words in an array; search / startsWith scan all of them.

approaches.name: Hash set (+ set of all prefixes)
approaches.idea: O(L) word lookup; prefix queries need every prefix of every word stored too.

approaches.name: Trie
approaches.idea: Nodes with a char → child map and an isEnd flag; walk one character at a time.
approaches.space: O(total chars) worst case, shared prefixes stored once

solution.summary: A trie is a tree where each edge is a character and each root-to-node path spells a prefix. Each node holds a map of children and an isEnd flag. Insert walks the word creating missing nodes and marks the end; search walks and checks isEnd; startsWith only checks that the walk succeeds. Every operation is O(L) for a word of length L.
solution.explanation:
**Structure.** `TrieNode = { children: char → TrieNode, isEnd: boolean }`. The root represents the empty prefix.

**insert(word)**
1. Start at the root.
2. For each character, create the child if it is missing, then move into it.
3. Mark the final node `isEnd = true`.

**search(word)** — walk the characters; if any is missing return false. At the end, return `isEnd` (the path existing is not enough: "ca" exists as a path because of "cat").

**startsWith(prefix)** — the same walk; return true if it completes. Sharing one `walk` helper keeps the code DRY.

**Children storage trade-off**
- **Array of 26** (Java version): fastest, but 26 pointers per node even if mostly empty.
- **Hash map** (JS / Python versions): memory proportional to actual children, supports any alphabet (Unicode, digits).

**Complexity.** Each operation touches one node per character: O(L), independent of how many words are stored. Space is O(total characters inserted) in the worst case; shared prefixes are stored once.

**Where tries are used:** autocomplete and search suggestions, spell checkers, IP routing (longest-prefix match), word games like Boggle (Word Search II).

complexity.time: O(L) per insert / search / startsWith — one step per character
complexity.space: O(total characters inserted) worst case; common prefixes are shared

keyPoints: Node = children map/array + isEnd flag
search needs isEnd; startsWith only needs the path to exist
O(L) per operation regardless of how many words are stored
Array[26] vs hash map: speed vs memory / alphabet flexibility
Real uses: autocomplete, spell check, longest-prefix match

visuals.title: Building and querying a trie with "cat", "car", "card", "dog"
visuals.caption: Each node is one character; ✓ marks isEnd. Green = newly created / successful match, light blue = reused path, red = failed check.

steps.note: An empty trie is a single root node with no children. Each edge below it will stand for one character; a path from the root spells a prefix.
insert("cat"): create 3 new nodes (c, a, t), then set `isEnd = true` on the last one (✓).
insert("car"): reuse the existing path c → a, create 1 new node (r), then set `isEnd = true` on the last one (✓).
insert("card"): reuse the existing path c → a → r, create 1 new node (d), then set `isEnd = true` on the last one (✓). "car" and "card" share the nodes c → a → r.
insert("dog"): create 3 new nodes (d, o, g), then set `isEnd = true` on the last one (✓).
search("car"): follow c → a → r. The node exists **and** has isEnd = true, so the result is true.
search("ca"): the path c → a exists, but no word ends at "a" (isEnd = false), so the result is false. "ca" is only a prefix.
startsWith("ca"): the same walk reaches "a". For a prefix query, existence of the node is enough → true.
search("cow"): "c" exists, but it has no child "o", so the walk returns null → false. We never touch the "dog" branch.

visuals.title: Trie vs hash set for word and prefix queries
rows: O(N · L) scan, or store all prefixes
List all words with a prefix
Walk to the prefix node, DFS below it
Shared prefixes stored once, but node overhead
Yes — DFS in alphabetical child order

pitfalls: Forgetting the isEnd flag, so search("ca") returns true after inserting "cat"
Using startsWith logic for search (or vice versa)
Creating a new child even when it exists, overwriting a whole subtree
Assuming only a–z with an array of 26 when the input can contain other characters

followUps.question: How would you support delete(word)?
followUps.answer: Walk to the word and clear isEnd; then, on the way back up (recursion), remove child nodes that have no children and are not the end of another word.

followUps.question: How do you return the top 3 autocomplete suggestions for a prefix?
followUps.answer: Walk to the prefix node and DFS in alphabetical order collecting words until you have 3; for speed, cache the top suggestions at each node at insert time.

followUps.question: How is a trie used in Word Search II?
followUps.answer: Insert all target words into a trie, then DFS the grid while walking the trie in parallel; prune as soon as the current path is not a prefix of any word.

questions.title: Same Tree
questions.prompt:
You are given the roots `p` and `q` of two binary trees. Return `true` if the trees are **identical** — exactly the same shape, with equal values in every matching position — and `false` otherwise.

Either tree may be empty.

examples.explanation: Same values, but 2 is a left child in p and a right child in q.
Everything matches except one leaf: 3 vs 5.

constraints: 0 ≤ number of nodes in each tree ≤ 100
hints: Two trees are identical when their roots are equal and … what must be true about their children?
Compare the pair (p, q), then recurse on the pair of left children and the pair of right children.
Handle the null cases first: both null → true, exactly one null → false. Only then compare the values.

approaches.name: Serialize both and compare strings
approaches.idea: Write each tree as a preorder string **with null markers** (e.g. `1,2,#,#,#`) and compare the strings. Correct, but builds two O(n) strings and walks both trees fully even when the roots already differ.

approaches.name: Recursive pairwise DFS
approaches.idea: isSameTree(p, q): null checks, compare values, then recurse on (p.left, q.left) and (p.right, q.right). Stops at the first mismatch.

approaches.name: Iterative with a queue of pairs
approaches.idea: Push (p, q); pop a pair, run the same checks, push its two child pairs. Same logic without deep recursion on skewed trees.

solution.summary: I compare the two trees pair by pair: two nulls are equal, exactly one null is a mismatch, otherwise the values must match and both the left pair and the right pair must be the same tree. It stops at the first difference — O(min(n, m)) time and O(h) recursion space.
solution.explanation:
**Think in pairs.** Walk both trees at the same time and always look at two nodes in the **same position**: (p, q), then (p.left, q.left), then (p.right, q.right).

**isSameTree(p, q)**
1. Both null → `true`: two empty trees are identical.
2. Exactly one null → `false`: one tree has a node where the other has none, so the **shapes** differ.
3. Values differ → `false`.
4. Otherwise return `isSameTree(p.left, q.left) && isSameTree(p.right, q.right)`.

**Order of the checks matters.** The null checks must come before `p.val` is read — otherwise you get a TypeError in JavaScript, a NullPointerException in Java or an AttributeError in Python.

**Why it is correct.** Two trees are identical exactly when the roots match and both pairs of subtrees are identical — which is the recursive case — and the two base cases cover every way a pair of positions can be empty.

**Early exit.** `&&` short-circuits: once the left subtrees differ, the right subtrees are never visited.

**Edge cases:** both empty → true; one empty → false; equal values in a mirrored shape (`[1, 2]` vs `[1, null, 2]`) → false; duplicate values are fine because we compare positions, not sets of values.

code.code:
function isSameTree(p, q) {
  if (!p && !q) return true;          // both empty: identical
  if (!p || !q) return false;         // only one empty: shapes differ
  if (p.val !== q.val) return false;  // values differ
  return isSameTree(p.left, q.left)   // left subtrees must match
    && isSameTree(p.right, q.right);  // and right subtrees too
}

public boolean isSameTree(TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    if (p == null && q == null) return true;   // both empty: identical
    if (p == null || q == null) return false;  // only one empty: shapes differ
    if (p.val != q.val) return false;          // values differ
    return isSameTree(p.left, q.left)          // left subtrees must match
        && isSameTree(p.right, q.right);       // and right subtrees too
}

complexity.time: O(min(n, m)) — each pair of matching positions is compared once and the walk stops at the first mismatch (O(n) when the trees are identical)
complexity.space: O(h) recursion depth, h = height of the shorter tree (O(n) for a skewed tree)

keyPoints: Compare positions pair by pair: (p, q), then (p.left, q.left) and (p.right, q.right)
Null checks before reading .val: both null → true, exactly one null → false
Shape matters as much as values
&& short-circuits on the first mismatch
The same skeleton solves Symmetric Tree (outer/inner pairs) and Subtree of Another Tree

visuals.title: isSameTree on p = [4, 2, 7, 1, 3] and q = [4, 2, 7, 1, 5]
visuals.caption: p is drawn on the left, q on the right. Blue = the pair being compared, orange = pairs waiting on the call stack, green = pairs that matched, red = the mismatch, grey = never visited.

steps.note: Call `isSameTree(p, q)` on the two roots (p is the tree on the left, q the one on the right). We will always compare **two nodes in the same position**.
Neither node is null and p.val = q.val = 4. The roots match, so the answer depends on the **left pair** and then the **right pair**: recurse on (p.left, q.left) first.
Next pair: p.val = q.val = 2, still equal. The pair (4, 4) waits on the call stack while we check (2, 2)'s children, left pair first.
p.val = q.val = 1, so recurse on the child pairs. Both are `(null, null)`, which return **true** at the first check — the pair (1, 1) matches completely.
The left pair matched, so (2, 2) now checks its **right pair**: p.val = 3 but q.val = 5. The values differ, so this call returns **false** immediately.

The false travels up. (2, 2) returns false because its right pair failed. Back in (4, 4) the left call returned false, so `&&` **short-circuits** and the right pair (7, 7) is never compared. `isSameTree` returns **false**.

visuals.title: Same values, different shape: p = [1, 2], q = [1, null, 2]
visuals.caption: p on the left, q on the right. Comparing plain traversals would wrongly say "same"; the pairwise null check catches the missing node.

steps.note: Both trees have the same values and the same plain preorder [1, 2] — a solution that only compares traversals would say **true**. In p the 2 is a **left** child, in q it is a **right** child.
Neither root is null and p.val = q.val = 1, so recurse on the left pair (p.left, q.left).
Left pair: p.left is 2 but q.left is null. Exactly one side is empty, so the **shapes differ** and the second check returns **false** — before any value is read.

`&&` short-circuits, so the root pair returns **false** without checking the right pair. A traversal-based solution must write a `#` for every null child (see the panels): then the two lists differ at index 1.

pitfalls: Reading p.val before checking whether p is null
Comparing traversal outputs without null markers — [1, 2] and [1, null, 2] both have preorder [1, 2]
Returning true as soon as the roots match, without checking both subtrees
Combining the left and right results with || instead of &&

followUps.question: Can you do it without recursion?
followUps.answer: Yes: use a queue (or stack) of pairs. Start with (p, q); pop a pair, run the same three checks, then push (p.left, q.left) and (p.right, q.right). Useful when the trees can be very deep.

followUps.question: How would you check whether one tree is the mirror image of another?
followUps.answer: Swap the pairing: compare (p.left, q.right) and (p.right, q.left). Symmetric Tree is exactly that check applied to root.left and root.right.

followUps.question: How would you check whether q appears somewhere inside p?
followUps.answer: Run isSameTree from every node of p (Subtree of Another Tree), O(n·m) worst case — or serialize both with null markers and use a linear-time string search.

questions.title: Subtree of Another Tree
questions.prompt:
You are given the roots of two binary trees, `root` and `subRoot`. Return `true` if `root` has a node whose **entire subtree** — that node together with all of its descendants — is identical to `subRoot` (same shape, same values). Otherwise return `false`.

Matching only the top part of a subtree does not count: the match must continue all the way down to the leaves.

examples.explanation: The subtree that starts at node 4 is exactly [4, 1, 2].

examples.input: root = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2, null, null, null, null, 0], subRoot = [4, 1, 2]
examples.explanation: Node 4’s subtree has an extra node 0 under 2, so it is [4, 1, 2, null, null, 0], not [4, 1, 2].
The root 1 has a child, so it does not match, but the leaf 1 does.

hints: Suppose you already had a function isSameTree(a, b). How would it help?
The copy of subRoot could start at any node of root. Try every node as a starting point.
isSubtree(root, sub) = isSameTree(root, sub) || isSubtree(root.left, sub) || isSubtree(root.right, sub), and an empty root returns false.

approaches.name: isSameTree from every node
approaches.idea: DFS over root; at each node run isSameTree(node, subRoot). Most starts fail at the first value comparison.
approaches.time: O(m·n) worst, m = nodes in root, n = nodes in subRoot

approaches.name: Serialize + substring search
approaches.idea: Serialize both trees in preorder with `#` for nulls and a separator before every value (`,4,1,#,#,2,#,#`), then check whether subRoot’s string occurs inside root’s string using KMP.

approaches.name: Subtree hashing (Merkle style)
approaches.idea: Compute a hash for every subtree bottom-up from (value, left hash, right hash) and compare with subRoot’s hash; confirm a hit with isSameTree to rule out collisions.

solution.summary: I try every node of root as a possible starting point and run isSameTree(node, subRoot) there; if any start matches, the answer is true. That is O(m·n) time in the worst case and O(h₁ + h₂) recursion space. If they ask for faster, I serialize both trees with null markers and use a linear-time substring search.
solution.explanation:
**Reduce it to a problem you already know.** "Is subRoot somewhere inside root?" means "is there a node X in root such that the tree starting at X is the **same tree** as subRoot?"

**Algorithm**
1. `isSubtree(null, subRoot)` → `false`: there are no nodes left to try.
2. If `isSameTree(root, subRoot)` → `true`: a match starts right here.
3. Otherwise try the children: `isSubtree(root.left, subRoot) || isSubtree(root.right, subRoot)`.

`isSameTree` is the standard pairwise check: both null → true; one null or different values → false; otherwise compare the left pairs and the right pairs.

**Why the whole subtree must match.** `isSameTree` is only true when both trees run out of nodes in exactly the same places. In the second example node 4 matches 4, 1 and 2, but the extra 0 under 2 meets a null in subRoot, so that start fails — exactly the definition of a subtree.

**Complexity.** Most candidates fail at the first value comparison, so typical runs are fast. The worst case is many near-matches: root is a long chain of 1s and subRoot is a chain of 1s ending in a 2 — every start walks deep before failing, giving O(m·n).

**Linear-time option (mention it).** Serialize both trees in preorder with `#` for null children and a separator **before** every value, e.g. `,4,1,#,#,2,#,#`. subRoot is a subtree of root exactly when its string occurs inside root's string, which KMP checks in O(m + n). The leading separator matters: without it, the value 2 would "match" the end of 12.

**Edge cases:** subRoot equal to the whole tree → true; a match must end where subRoot's leaves end (`[1, 1]` vs `[1]` matches the leaf, not the root); duplicate values are fine because every start is checked.
