complexity.time: O(m·n) worst case — up to m starting nodes, each comparison up to n nodes (most starts fail at the first value)
complexity.space: O(h₁ + h₂) — recursion down root plus the nested isSameTree recursion down subRoot

keyPoints: Reuse isSameTree: a subtree match is a same-tree check that starts at some node
Try every node: isSameTree(root, sub) || isSubtree(root.left, sub) || isSubtree(root.right, sub)
The match must cover the whole subtree down to the leaves, not just the top part
Worst case O(m·n); mention serialization + KMP or subtree hashing for O(m + n)
When serializing, include null markers and a separator before every value

visuals.title: isSubtree on root = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2, 4, null, null, null, 0, null, 1, 2], subRoot = [4, 1, 2]
visuals.caption: root on the left, subRoot on the right. Orange = current candidate start, blue = pair being compared, green = matched, red = mismatch, grey = rejected candidates.

steps.note: root is on the left, subRoot on the right. Any node of root could be where a copy of subRoot starts, so `isSubtree` tries the nodes one by one (preorder) and asks `isSameTree(candidate, subRoot)`.
Candidate 3: `isSameTree(3, 4)` fails at once because p.val = 3 ≠ q.val = 4. No match starts here, so `isSubtree` moves on to the left child.
Candidate 4: p.val = q.val = 4, so this could be the start of a match. `isSameTree` now walks both trees together: left pair first, then right pair.
Pair (1, 1): equal, and both child pairs are `(null, null)` → true. This part of subRoot is matched.
Pair (2, 2): equal, keep going into its children (left pair first).

Pair (0, null): root has a node 0 where subRoot has **nothing**, so `isSameTree` returns false. A near miss — the top three nodes matched, but a subtree must match **all the way down**. Candidate 4 fails.

Candidates 1, 2, 0 and 5 (continuing in preorder) all fail at the **very first** comparison: their values are not 4. Their null children return false at `if (!root)`. Cheap rejections like these are the common case.
Candidate 4: p.val = q.val = 4, so this could be the start of a match. `isSameTree` now walks both trees together: left pair first, then right pair.
Pair (1, 1): equal, and both child pairs are `(null, null)` → true. This part of subRoot is matched.
Pair (2, 2): equal, and both child pairs are `(null, null)` → true. This part of subRoot is matched.

Every pair matched and every null lined up with a null, so `isSameTree(4, subRoot)` is true and `isSubtree` returns **true** at this candidate. The `||` short-circuits all the way up — no more nodes are tried.

visuals.title: Three ways to find a subtree
rows: Try each node of root as a start; compare with subRoot pair by pair
Preorder strings with # for nulls and a separator before every value; is sub’s string inside root’s?
Hash each subtree from (value, left hash, right hash); look for subRoot’s hash
O(m + n) with KMP; O(m·n) with a naive search
Stopping when the root fails instead of trying its children
No separator: "2" matches inside "12"; no # markers: shapes look equal
Hash collisions — confirm a hit with isSameTree
Follow-up on many queries or huge trees

pitfalls: Returning false as soon as the root fails isSameTree instead of also trying its children
Accepting a match of only the top part of a subtree (ignoring extra descendants)
Serializing without null markers or without a leading separator — different shapes look equal and 2 matches inside 12
Missing the empty-root base case, which crashes on root.left

followUps.question: What if subRoot is empty (null)?
followUps.answer: By convention the empty tree is a subtree of every tree, so return true — but confirm with the interviewer. The code above would return false, so add `if (!subRoot) return true` at the top if needed.

followUps.question: Can you make it linear?
followUps.answer: Serialize both trees in preorder with null markers and a leading separator (e.g. `,3,4,1,#,#,2,#,#,5,#,#`) and search for subRoot’s string inside root’s with KMP: O(m + n). Alternatively hash every subtree bottom-up and compare hashes, confirming a hit with isSameTree.

followUps.question: What if subRoot only has to match the top part of some subtree (extra descendants allowed)?
followUps.answer: Relax the comparison: when the subRoot side is null, return true no matter what the root side has; return false only when the root side is null but the subRoot side is not, or the values differ.

questions.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
questions.pattern: Divide and conquer on traversal ranges
questions.prompt:
You are given two traversals of the same binary tree as integer arrays: `preorder` (node, left, right) and `inorder` (left, node, right). All values in the tree are **distinct**.

Rebuild the tree and return its root.

examples.explanation: 1 comes first in preorder, so it is the root. In inorder, [4, 2, 5] is to its left (left subtree) and [3, 6] to its right (right subtree). Repeat inside each part.
Each root is the last value of its inorder range, so every right subtree is empty: a left-leaning chain.

constraints: All values are distinct, and both arrays come from the same tree
hints: Which of the two arrays tells you the root immediately?
preorder[0] is the root. Find it in inorder — what do the values to its left and to its right represent?

If the root sits at index mid of inorder[lo..hi], the left subtree is inorder[lo..mid−1] and the right subtree is inorder[mid+1..hi]. Keep one running index into preorder and build the left subtree before the right.
Scanning inorder for every root costs O(n) each time — precompute a value → index hash map.

approaches.name: Recursion with slicing and linear search
approaches.idea: Root = preorder[0]; find it with indexOf in inorder; slice both arrays into left and right parts and recurse. Easy to write, but every level scans and copies arrays.

approaches.name: Index map + range boundaries
approaches.idea: Precompute value → inorder index. build(lo, hi) takes the next preorder value as the root, splits at mid = pos[root], then builds lo..mid−1 and mid+1..hi. No copying, O(1) per node.

approaches.name: Iterative with a stack
approaches.idea: Walk preorder keeping a stack of nodes whose right child is still unknown. While the stack top differs from the next unmatched inorder value, the new node is the top’s left child; otherwise pop while the top matches inorder and attach the new node as the right child of the last popped node.

solution.summary: preorder[0] is the root, and its position in inorder splits the other values into the left subtree (before it) and the right subtree (after it). I recurse on those inorder ranges, taking each root from preorder with one running index and finding it in inorder with a precomputed hash map — O(n) time and O(n) space.
solution.explanation:
**Two facts do all the work**
- In **preorder** the root comes first: `[root, ...left subtree..., ...right subtree...]`.
- In **inorder** the root sits between its subtrees: `[...left subtree..., root, ...right subtree...]`.

So the first preorder value is the root, and its index `mid` in inorder tells you exactly which values form the left subtree (`inorder[lo..mid−1]`) and which form the right subtree (`inorder[mid+1..hi]`).

**Algorithm**
1. Build a map `pos`: value → index in `inorder` (well defined because values are distinct).
2. Keep a pointer `pre` into `preorder`: the next value to use as a root.
3. `build(lo, hi)` builds the tree whose inorder is `inorder[lo..hi]`:
   - if `lo > hi` the range is empty → return `null`;
   - `val = preorder[pre++]` is this subtree's root and `mid = pos[val]`;
   - `node.left = build(lo, mid − 1)`, **then** `node.right = build(mid + 1, hi)`.
4. Return `build(0, n − 1)`.

**Why left before right?** Preorder lists the **whole left subtree before the right subtree**. Because `pre` is shared, building the left side first consumes exactly the left subtree's values (there are `mid − lo` of them) and leaves `pre` on the right subtree's root. Swapping the two calls builds a wrong tree.

**Why the hash map?** Without it, finding `val` in inorder is an O(n) scan per node, which is O(n²) on a skewed tree. With it every node costs O(1).

**Why distinct values?** With duplicates, a root value could appear several times in inorder, the split point would be ambiguous, and different trees could produce the same pair of traversals.

**Edge cases:** a single node; skewed trees (one side of every split is empty, so that call hits `lo > hi` immediately); negative values need no special handling.

code.code:
def build_tree(preorder, inorder):
    pos = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}  # value -> index in inorder
    pre = 0                                      # next root in preorder

    def build(lo, hi):                           # tree for inorder[lo..hi]
        nonlocal pre
        if lo > hi:
            return None                          # empty range: no node
        val = preorder[pre]                      # preorder gives the root
        pre += 1
        mid = pos[val]                           # root splits inorder in two
        node = TreeNode(val)
        node.left = build(lo, mid - 1)           # left part first (preorder!)
        node.right = build(mid + 1, hi)
        return node

    return build(0, len(inorder) - 1)

complexity.time: O(n) — each node is created once and its inorder position is an O(1) map lookup
complexity.space: O(n) — the map, plus O(h) recursion depth (O(n) for a skewed tree)

keyPoints: preorder[0] is the root; its inorder index splits the left and right subtrees
The left subtree has mid − lo nodes, so it uses the next mid − lo preorder values
Precompute a value → index map to avoid O(n²) searching
One shared preorder pointer; build the left subtree before the right
Needs distinct values; preorder + postorder alone is not enough in general

visuals.title: How each root splits inorder: preorder = [1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 6], inorder = [4, 2, 5, 1, 3, 6]
visuals.caption: One step per build(lo, hi) call that creates a node. Blue = the root of this call, light-blue range = its left subtree, orange range = its right subtree, grey = values outside this call (or preorder values already used).

steps.note: `preorder` lists every root **before** its subtrees, so `preorder[0]` is the root of the whole tree. `inorder` lists every root **between** its left and right subtrees. The first call covers the full inorder range [0..5].

build(0, 5): root = preorder[0] = **1**, found at inorder index mid = 3. Left of it: [4, 2, 5] → the left subtree, which uses the next 3 values of preorder (2, 4, 5). Right of it: [3, 6] → the right subtree.
build(0, 2): root = preorder[1] = **2**, found at inorder index mid = 1. Left of it: [4] → the left subtree, which uses the next 1 value of preorder (4). Right of it: [5] → the right subtree.
build(0, 0): root = preorder[2] = **4**, found at inorder index mid = 0. Both sides of it are empty, so it is a leaf.
build(2, 2): root = preorder[3] = **5**, found at inorder index mid = 2. Both sides of it are empty, so it is a leaf.
build(4, 5): root = preorder[4] = **3**, found at inorder index mid = 4. Left of it: nothing (empty left subtree). Right of it: [6] → the right subtree.
build(5, 5): root = preorder[5] = **6**, found at inorder index mid = 5. Both sides of it are empty, so it is a leaf.
`pre` has walked off the end: each preorder value became the root of exactly one range. The result is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, null, 6] — O(n) total because each `pos.get` is O(1).

visuals.title: The tree growing, one build(lo, hi) call at a time
visuals.caption: Blue = node created in this step, orange = calls still on the stack (waiting for a subtree), light blue = finished subtrees. Panels: the preorder value just used and the inorder range of the current call.

steps.note: The map `pos` (value → index in inorder) is ready and `pre = 0`. Start with `build(0, 5)`: the whole inorder array is one tree whose root we do not know yet.

build(0, 5): the next preorder value `preorder[0] = 1` is this range's root, and `pos.get(1)` = 3. It is the root of the whole tree. Left of it: [4, 2, 5] → left subtree; right of it: [3, 6] → right subtree. Build the left one first.

build(0, 2): the next preorder value `preorder[1] = 2` is this range's root, and `pos.get(2)` = 1. It becomes 1.left. Left of it: [4] → left subtree; right of it: [5] → right subtree. Build the left one first.
build(0, 0): the next preorder value `preorder[2] = 4` is this range's root, and `pos.get(4)` = 0. It becomes 2.left. Nothing is on either side, so it is a leaf (both child calls get empty ranges).

Inside build(0, 0) for 4: the left call is build(0, -1) and the right call is build(1, 0). Both ranges are **empty** (lo > hi), so both return null — 4 is a leaf. Notice `pre` did not move: empty ranges consume nothing.
build(2, 2): the next preorder value `preorder[3] = 5` is this range's root, and `pos.get(5)` = 2. It becomes 2.right. Nothing is on either side, so it is a leaf (both child calls get empty ranges).

build(4, 5): the next preorder value `preorder[4] = 3` is this range's root, and `pos.get(3)` = 4. It becomes 1.right. Left of it: nothing (build(4, 3) is empty → null). Right of it: [6] → right subtree.
build(5, 5): the next preorder value `preorder[5] = 6` is this range's root, and `pos.get(6)` = 5. It becomes 3.right. Nothing is on either side, so it is a leaf (both child calls get empty ranges).
Every call has returned and `pre = 6`: all preorder values were used exactly once. `buildTree` returns the root 1; in level order the tree is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, null, 6].

pitfalls: Building the right subtree first while using a shared preorder pointer
Searching inorder with indexOf for every node — O(n²) on skewed trees
Off-by-one ranges: left is lo..mid − 1 and right is mid + 1..hi, both inclusive
Slicing arrays in every call — correct, but O(n²) copying in the worst case

followUps.question: How would you build it from inorder and postorder instead?
followUps.answer: Postorder ends with the root, so walk postorder from the end with a decreasing pointer and build the **right** subtree before the left, using the same inorder index map.

followUps.question: Can preorder and postorder rebuild the tree?
followUps.answer: Not uniquely in general: a root 1 with 2 as its left child and a root 1 with 2 as its right child both give preorder [1, 2] and postorder [2, 1]. It works only for full binary trees, where every node has 0 or 2 children.

followUps.question: Can you do it without recursion?
followUps.answer: Yes, with a stack: walk preorder; while the stack top differs from the next unmatched inorder value, attach the new node as the top’s left child; otherwise pop while the top equals the inorder value (advancing in inorder) and attach the new node as the right child of the last popped node. Push the new node each time. O(n).

questions.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
questions.pattern: Tree DFS: return one branch, record both
questions.prompt:
In a binary tree, a **path** is a sequence of nodes in which every two consecutive nodes are joined by an edge and no node appears twice. A path contains **at least one node**; it does not have to pass through the root or end at a leaf. Its **path sum** is the sum of its node values.

Given the `root` of a binary tree whose values may be **negative**, return the largest path sum of any path.

examples.explanation: The path 9 → −6 → 8 bends at −6. It beats every path through the root, e.g. 9 → −6 → 1 → 3 = 7.
The path 1 → 2 → 3.
All values are negative, so the best path is the single node −1.

hints: Every path has one highest node where it "bends". What does the best path bending at a given node look like?
It is node.val, plus the best path going down into the left child, plus the best path going down into the right child — each only if it helps (is positive).
Define gain(node) = best sum of a path that starts at node and goes down. A parent can extend only one side, so gain = node.val + max(0, gainL, gainR).
In the same postorder DFS, update a global best with node.val + max(0, gainL) + max(0, gainR). Start best at −∞, not 0.

approaches.name: DFS from every node
approaches.idea: Treat the tree as an undirected graph; from every node run a DFS that accumulates the sum to every other node and track the maximum. Covers every path, but repeats a lot of work.

approaches.name: Best bend per node, recomputed
approaches.idea: For each node, compute the best downward path of each child with a separate DFS, then combine. Correct, but the downward sums are recomputed for every ancestor.
approaches.time: O(n²) worst (skewed), O(n log n) balanced

approaches.name: Single postorder DFS
approaches.idea: gain(node) returns node.val + max(left, right) with negative child gains clamped to 0, and records node.val + left + right in a global best.

solution.summary: One postorder DFS. gain(node) returns the best path that starts at node and goes down one side — node.val + max(left, right), where each child gain is clamped at 0. At every node I also record the best path that bends there, node.val + left + right, in a global best that starts at −∞. O(n) time, O(h) space.
solution.explanation:
**Every path has a top.** Any path has exactly one highest node, where it bends. The best path that bends at node X is X's value, plus the best downward path into X's left subtree, plus the best downward path into X's right subtree — **each included only if it is positive**.

**Two different quantities per node**
- What we **return** to the parent: `gain(X) = X.val + max(left, right)`. The parent can continue the path into **one** side only — a path cannot fork.
- What we **record**: `X.val + left + right`, the path that bends at X and uses both sides.

Here `left = max(0, gain(X.left))` and `right = max(0, gain(X.right))`: a negative branch would only lower the sum, so we take 0 instead (= do not extend that way).

**Algorithm**
1. `best = −∞` (a path must contain at least one node).
2. `gain(null) = 0`.
3. For a node: compute `left` and `right` from the children (clamped at 0), update `best = max(best, node.val + left + right)`, and return `node.val + max(left, right)`.
4. After `gain(root)`, return `best`.

**Why −∞ and not 0?** If every value is negative, the answer is the largest single value (e.g. −1). Starting at 0 would return 0 — the sum of an *empty* path, which is not allowed.

**Clamp the children, not the node.** `gain(X)` itself may be negative (e.g. a negative leaf); we still return it honestly and let the **parent** decide with `max(0, …)` whether to use it. The node's own value is never dropped, so every recorded candidate contains at least one node.

**Why it is correct.** Every path is considered at its unique top node, and there the best choice on each side is exactly the clamped best downward gain — so `best` ends up as the maximum over all paths.

**Overflow:** with at most 3·10⁴ nodes of absolute value ≤ 1000, every sum stays within ±3·10⁷, far inside a 32-bit int.

code.code:
def max_path_sum(root):
    best = float('-inf')                   # a path has at least one node

    def gain(node):                        # best downward path from node
        nonlocal best
        if not node:
            return 0
        left = max(0, gain(node.left))     # drop negative branches
        right = max(0, gain(node.right))
        best = max(best, node.val + left + right)  # path that bends here
        return node.val + max(left, right)         # parent may use one side

    gain(root)
    return best

complexity.time: O(n) — every node is visited once with O(1) work
complexity.space: O(h) recursion depth — O(log n) for a balanced tree, O(n) for a skewed one

keyPoints: Every path has exactly one top node where it bends
Return node.val + max(left, right); record node.val + left + right
Clamp child gains with max(0, …) to drop negative branches
Initialise best to −∞ (or the root’s value), never 0
Same skeleton as Diameter of a Binary Tree, with sums instead of heights

visuals.title: gain() on [1, -6, 3, 9, 8, null, -2]
visuals.caption: Finished nodes show `value (g=gain returned)`. Blue = current call, orange = ancestors waiting on the call stack, light blue = finished, green = best path so far, grey = branch dropped by max(0, …).

steps.note: Start with `best = −∞`. A postorder DFS computes `gain(node)` — the best path that starts at node and goes **down** — for the children first, then for the node itself.
Leaf 9: both children are null, so left = right = 0. Path bending here: 9 + 0 + 0 = 9 — a new best, **best = 9** (just the node 9). Return 9 + max(0, 0) = 9 to the parent.
Leaf 8: both children are null, so left = right = 0. Path bending here: 8 + 0 + 0 = 8, not better than best = 9. Return 8 + max(0, 0) = 8 to the parent.
Node -6: gain(9) = 9, gain(8) = 8. So left = 9, right = 8. Path bending here: -6 + 9 + 8 = 11 — a new best, **best = 11** (path 9 → -6 → 8). Return -6 + max(9, 8) = 3 to the parent.
Leaf -2: both children are null, so left = right = 0. Path bending here: -2 + 0 + 0 = -2, not better than best = 11. Return -2 + max(0, 0) = -2 to the parent.

Node 3: left child is null → 0, gain(-2) = -2. **-2 would only lower the sum**, so max(0, …) drops it: left = 0, right = 0. Path bending here: 3 + 0 + 0 = 3, not better than best = 11. Return 3 + max(0, 0) = 3 to the parent.
Node 1: gain(-6) = 3, gain(3) = 3. So left = 3, right = 3. Path bending here: 1 + 3 + 3 = 7, not better than best = 11. Return 1 + max(3, 3) = 4 to the parent.

`gain(root)` is done and `maxPathSum` returns **11**: the path 9 → -6 → 8 bends at -6 and does not touch the root. The best path through the root (9 → -6 → 1 → 3) only reaches 7, and the negative leaf -2 was never worth adding.

visuals.title: All values negative: [-3, -5, -1]
visuals.caption: Why best must start at −∞: here every path sum is negative. Green = best path so far, grey = branch dropped by max(0, …).

steps.note: Same algorithm on a tree where **every value is negative**. `best` starts at −∞, so the first candidate always replaces it.
Leaf -5: both children are null, so left = right = 0. Path bending here: -5 + 0 + 0 = -5 — a new best, **best = -5** (just the node -5). Return -5 + max(0, 0) = -5 to the parent.
Leaf -1: both children are null, so left = right = 0. Path bending here: -1 + 0 + 0 = -1 — a new best, **best = -1** (just the node -1). Return -1 + max(0, 0) = -1 to the parent.

Node -3: gain(-5) = -5, gain(-1) = -1. **-5 and -1 would only lower the sum**, so max(0, …) drops them: left = 0, right = 0. Path bending here: -3 + 0 + 0 = -3, not better than best = -1. Return -3 + max(0, 0) = -3 to the parent.
`maxPathSum` returns **-1** — the single node -1. Had `best` started at 0, the answer would be 0, the sum of an empty path, which is not a valid path.

visuals.title: Same skeleton as Diameter: return one side, record both
rows: left + right (edges of the path bending here)
−∞ (a path must contain at least one node)

pitfalls: Returning node.val + left + right to the parent — a path cannot fork into both children
Starting best at 0, which returns 0 for an all-negative tree
Clamping the node’s own value or the returned gain instead of the child gains
Only considering paths that go through the root or end at a leaf

followUps.question: How would you return the path itself, not just the sum?
followUps.answer: At each node remember which child gave the larger (positive) gain. When best improves at node X, store X. Afterwards build the path by walking down from X.left and from X.right, always following the remembered better child while its gain is positive, and join the two halves through X.

followUps.question: What if the path must go from the root down to a leaf?
followUps.answer: Much simpler: f(leaf) = leaf.val and f(node) = node.val + max over its existing children of f(child), with no clamping (the path must reach a leaf). The answer is f(root).

followUps.question: What if the tree is very deep?
followUps.answer: Recursion depth equals the height, up to 3·10⁴ for a chain. Python’s default recursion limit is 1000, so raise it with sys.setrecursionlimit or switch to an iterative postorder with an explicit stack that stores each node’s gain.

questions.title: Serialize and Deserialize a Binary Tree
questions.prompt:
Design two functions:
- `serialize(root)` turns a binary tree into a **string**;
- `deserialize(data)` turns that string back into the **same tree** (same shape, same values).

You choose the format. The only requirement is that `deserialize(serialize(root))` reproduces the original tree for every input, including the empty tree. Values can be negative and have several digits, and neither function may keep state between calls.

examples.explanation: Preorder with # for every missing child: 5 nodes give 2·5 + 1 = 11 tokens.
A right-leaning chain: every left child is #.

hints: A single traversal such as preorder [1, 2, 3] fits many different trees. What extra information removes the ambiguity?
Write a marker such as # for every null child. Then the preorder sequence alone pins down the shape.
Separate tokens with commas so that -3 and 12 stay single tokens.

To deserialize, read tokens in the same preorder: a number creates a node, then build its left subtree, then its right; # returns null. One shared index (or iterator) over the tokens is all the state you need.

approaches.name: Two traversals (preorder + inorder)
approaches.idea: Store both traversals and rebuild with the split-by-root algorithm. Needs distinct values and stores 2n numbers.

approaches.name: Level order (BFS) with null markers
approaches.idea: Write nodes level by level with # for missing children (the format LeetCode uses to print trees). Deserialize with a queue: each dequeued node takes the next two tokens as its children. Fully iterative.

approaches.name: Preorder DFS with null markers
approaches.idea: Write node, left, right with # for nulls; read it back with the same recursion and a shared index. The shortest code; every token is read exactly once.

solution.summary: I serialize with a preorder DFS, writing each value and a # for every null child, separated by commas. To deserialize I read the tokens in the same preorder with a shared index: a number creates a node and recursively builds its left and then its right subtree, and # returns null. Both directions are O(n) time and space.
solution.explanation:
**Why null markers?** A preorder list like `1, 2, 3` fits many trees (2 could be a left or a right child). Writing `#` for every missing child records the shape: a tree with n nodes has exactly n + 1 null children, so the string has 2n + 1 tokens and describes exactly one tree.

**serialize**
1. Preorder DFS: at a null node append `#`; otherwise append the value, then recurse left, then right.
2. Join the tokens with `,`. The separator keeps `-3` and `12` as single tokens.

**deserialize**
1. Split on `,` and keep an index `i` to the next unread token.
2. `build()`: read `tok = tokens[i++]`. If it is `#`, return `null`. Otherwise create the node, then `node.left = build()` and `node.right = build()` — the **same order** the serializer used.
3. Return `build()`.

**Why it works.** The serializer writes a subtree as its value, then the complete encoding of its left subtree, then the complete encoding of its right subtree. When the recursive `build()` for the left subtree returns, it has read exactly that subtree's tokens (each node it creates is closed by its two child encodings), so `i` points at the start of the right subtree. Every token is read exactly once.

**Example.** `[7, -3, 12, null, 5, 10]` → `7,-3,#,5,#,#,12,10,#,#,#`. Reading it back: 7 is the root; -3 is its left child; `#` says -3 has no left child; 5 is -3's right child and its two `#`s close it; 12 is 7's right child; 10 is 12's left child; the final `#` is 12's missing right child.

**State.** The index must be shared by all recursive calls — a closure variable in JavaScript, an iterator in Python and Java. Passing a plain int down the recursion does not work, because the caller would not see how far the callee advanced.

**Practical notes.** Recursion depth equals the tree height, so a very deep (skewed) tree can overflow the call stack — Python's default limit is 1000 frames; the BFS format avoids recursion entirely. In real systems you would use JSON or a binary format such as Protocol Buffers for the same job.

complexity.time: O(n) — each node and each null marker is written once and read once (2n + 1 tokens)
complexity.space: O(n) — the string and token list, plus O(h) recursion depth

keyPoints: One traversal alone is ambiguous; null markers make preorder unambiguous
Use a separator so negative and multi-digit values stay single tokens
Deserialize in exactly the order you serialized: node, left, right
A shared index or iterator over the tokens is the only state needed
n nodes → 2n + 1 tokens; O(n) time and space in both directions

visuals.title: serialize: preorder with null markers on [7, -3, 12, null, 5, 10]
visuals.caption: Blue = node being written, orange = ancestors waiting on the call stack, light blue = already written. The `out` panel grows one token at a time; # marks a missing child.

steps.note: Serialize with a **preorder** DFS (node, left, right). Every missing child will be written as `#`, so the string records the shape as well as the values. Start with an empty `out`.
Visit the root: write "7" first (preorder), then serialize its left subtree, then its right subtree.
Visit -3: write "-3" — the comma separators will keep multi-digit and negative values as single tokens. Its parent 7 waits on the call stack.
-3 has no left child: `dfs(null)` writes **#**. Without this marker, the next value (5) would be read back as -3's left child instead of its right child.
Visit 5 (-3's right child): write "5". It is a leaf, so `dfs(node.left)` and `dfs(node.right)` both hit null and write `#`, `#` — every leaf ends with two markers.
Visit 12: write "12". Its parent 7 waits on the call stack.
Visit 10 (12's left child): write "10". It is a leaf, so `dfs(node.left)` and `dfs(node.right)` both hit null and write `#`, `#` — every leaf ends with two markers.
12 has no right child: `dfs(null)` writes **#**. Every missing child gets a marker — even the last one — so the reader knows this slot is empty.
Done: 5 nodes produced 11 tokens (2·5 + 1 — a tree with n nodes has n + 1 null children). Join them with commas: **"7,-3,#,5,#,#,12,10,#,#,#"**.

visuals.title: deserialize: rebuilding from "7,-3,#,5,#,#,12,10,#,#,#"
visuals.caption: The tokens panel highlights what this step reads; the call stack shows which child slot the current build() call is filling. Blue = node just created (or whose child slot was just set to null), orange = waiting ancestors, light blue = finished.

steps.note: Split the string on commas into 11 tokens and set `i = 0`. `build()` reads tokens in the **same preorder** the serializer wrote them.
Read "7" → create node 7; it is the **root**. Now build its left subtree from the following tokens, then its right subtree.
Read "-3" → create node -3; it fills the slot **7.left**. Now build its left subtree from the following tokens, then its right subtree.
Read "#" → `build()` returns null, so **-3.left = null**. The next token will go to -3.right.
Read "5" → create node 5; it fills the slot **-3.right**. The next two tokens are `#`, `#`: its left and right calls return null, so 5 is a leaf.
Read "12" → create node 12; it fills the slot **7.right**. Now build its left subtree from the following tokens, then its right subtree.
Read "10" → create node 10; it fills the slot **12.left**. The next two tokens are `#`, `#`: its left and right calls return null, so 10 is a leaf.
Read "#" → `build()` returns null, so **12.right = null**. 12 is complete.
All 11 tokens were read exactly once (i = 11) and every call has returned. The rebuilt tree is [7, -3, 12, null, 5, 10] — identical to the original.

rows: Queue: each dequeued node takes the next two tokens as its children
Split by root with an index map (Construct from Preorder and Inorder)
Not allowed — the split would be ambiguous
O(h) depth — a very deep tree can overflow the stack

pitfalls: Omitting null markers — the shape cannot be recovered
Reading the string character by character instead of comma-separated tokens, which breaks on -3 or 12
Building the right subtree before the left when reading a preorder string
Passing the index as a plain int parameter in Java/Python, so recursive calls never advance the caller’s position
Forgetting the empty tree: serialize(null) should give "#" and deserialize("#") should give null

followUps.question: How would you do it with BFS instead?
followUps.answer: Serialize level by level with a queue, writing # for missing children. To deserialize, create the root from the first token and enqueue it; for each dequeued node, read the next two tokens as its left and right children and enqueue the non-null ones.

followUps.question: Can you make the string shorter if the tree is a BST?
followUps.answer: Yes: a BST with distinct values is determined by its preorder alone, so no null markers are needed. Rebuild it in O(n) by reading preorder values with (low, high) bounds — a value outside the current bounds belongs to an ancestor’s other subtree.

followUps.question: How would you serialize an N-ary tree?
followUps.answer: Write each node’s value followed by its number of children (or close each child list with an end marker). To deserialize, read the value and the count, then build that many children recursively.

questions.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
questions.prompt:
Design a data structure that supports adding new words and checking if a string matches any previously added word:

- `WordDictionary()` initializes the object.
- `addWord(word)` adds `word` to the data structure.
- `search(word)` returns `true` if there is any string in the data structure that matches `word`, or `false` otherwise. `word` may contain dots `.` where a dot can match **any single letter**.

examples.input: addWord("bad"), addWord("dad"), addWord("mad"), search("pad"), search("bad"), search(".ad"), search("b..")
examples.explanation: ".ad" matches "bad", "dad", or "mad". "b.." matches "bad".

constraints: word in addWord consists of lowercase English letters.
word in search consists of "." or lowercase English letters (at most 2 dots per query).
At most 10^4 calls will be made to addWord and search.
hints: A standard Trie handles exact prefix/word lookups in O(L) time. How does `.` change the traversal?
When the current character is a regular letter `ch`, follow the single child `node.children[ch]` as usual.
When the current character is `.`, recursively DFS across **all** children of the current Trie node and return `true` if any branch succeeds.

approaches.name: Group words by length + linear regex scan
approaches.idea: Store words in a bucket by length and compare character by character on each `search`. Slow when many words share the same length.

approaches.name: Trie with recursive DFS on "." wildcard (Optimal)
approaches.idea: Insert each word into a Trie in O(L). For `search`, walk deterministically on normal characters and branch via DFS across all existing child nodes whenever you encounter `.`.
approaches.time: O(L) exact, O(26^d · L) with d dots

solution.summary: Back the dictionary with a Trie. `addWord` inserts characters in O(L). `search` runs a helper `dfs(node, index)` that steps into `node.children[ch]` for a normal letter or tries every child of `node` when the character is `.`.
solution.explanation:
A **Trie (Prefix Tree)** shares common prefixes across words, making exact steps O(1) per character:

1. **TrieNode**: holds a map/object `children` and a boolean `isWord = false`.
2. **`addWord(word)`**: walk from `root`, creating child nodes as needed, and set `node.isWord = true` at the end.
3. **`search(word)`**: call `dfs(root, 0)`:
   - Base case: if `i === word.length`, return `node.isWord`.
   - If `word[i] === "."`, loop over every child in `Object.values(node.children)` and if `dfs(child, i + 1)` is `true`, return `true`.
   - Otherwise, look up `next = node.children[word[i]]`; if missing return `false`, else return `dfs(next, i + 1)`.

complexity.time: O(L) for addWord and exact search; O(26^d · L) when the query has d wildcard dots.
complexity.space: O(T) to store T total Trie nodes, plus O(L) recursion stack during search.

keyPoints: A `.` only branches across children that actually exist in `node.children`, not all 26 letters if sparse.
Always check `node.isWord` at `i === word.length` so prefixes of longer words don’t falsely match.
Iterative traversal works for exact characters, while recursion cleanly handles branching at `.`.

visuals.title: Searching ".ad" in a Trie containing "bad" and "dad"
visuals.caption: At index 0, "." branches to children "b" and "d"; the first branch to reach a word-end at index 3 returns true.

steps.note: Trie after inserting `"bad"` and `"dad"`. We start `search(".ad")` at `root` with index `i = 0`.
Since `word[0] === "."`, we branch into the first child `"b"` and advance to `i = 1` (`"a"`).
At `i = 1` (`"a"`) and `i = 2` (`"d"`), we follow exact children `b → a → d*` where `isWord = true`. Search returns `true`!

pitfalls: Returning `true` when `i === word.length` without checking `node.isWord` (matches a prefix instead of a full word).
Continuing the loop without returning `true` when one `.` DFS branch succeeds.

followUps.question: How would you speed up searches like `"....a"` where all wildcards are at the beginning?
followUps.answer: Maintain a second Trie of **reversed** words, or partition Tries by word length so searches that fail length checks bail out in O(1).

quiz.question: What does an inorder traversal of a valid binary search tree produce?
options: The root first, then the leaves
quiz.explanation: Inorder visits left subtree, node, right subtree. In a BST everything on the left is smaller and everything on the right is larger, so the values come out ascending. Descending would be reverse inorder (right, node, left).

quiz.question: You need to free every node of a tree, and a node must only be freed after its children. Which traversal fits?
quiz.explanation: Postorder processes both subtrees before the node itself, so children are always handled first. Preorder would free the parent while you still need its child pointers.

quiz.question: You insert 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 (in that order) into an empty, non-balancing BST. What is the worst-case cost of a search afterwards?
options: O(n) — the tree is a chain of right children
O(log n) — BST search is always logarithmic
O(1) — the root is the median
quiz.explanation: Sorted inserts always go right, producing a linked-list-shaped tree of height n. BST operations are O(h), and here h = n. Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) prevent this.

quiz.question: Which data structure does a level-order (breadth-first) traversal use?
quiz.explanation: A FIFO queue returns nodes in the order they were discovered: the root, then depth 1, then depth 2, and so on. A stack gives depth-first order instead.

quiz.question: A binary tree has height h, counted as the number of nodes on its longest root-to-leaf path. What is the maximum number of nodes it can have?
quiz.explanation: Level i holds at most 2^i nodes (i = 0 … h − 1), and 1 + 2 + … + 2^(h−1) = 2^h − 1. A perfect tree reaches this bound.

quiz.question: Why is checking `node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val` at every node NOT enough to validate a BST?
options: A deeper node can still violate the bound set by a higher ancestor
It does not handle empty trees
It rejects trees with negative values
quiz.explanation: In [8, 4, 12, 2, 9], node 9 is a valid right child of 4 but sits in 8’s left subtree, so it must be < 8. You need (low, high) bounds from all ancestors, or a strictly increasing inorder traversal.

quiz.question: When deleting a BST node that has two children, what is the standard replacement value?
options: The largest value in its right subtree
Its inorder successor — the smallest value in its right subtree
quiz.explanation: The inorder successor (leftmost node of the right subtree) is larger than everything on the left and no larger than anything remaining on the right, so the BST order is kept. The inorder predecessor works too; the largest value of the right subtree would break the order.

quiz.question: What is the extra space used by a recursive DFS over a tree with n nodes and height h?
quiz.explanation: At any moment the call stack holds one root-to-node path, so O(h). That is O(log n) only for balanced trees and O(n) for a skewed one — which is why “always O(log n)” is wrong.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.explanation: walk recurses left, then right, then records the node — a postorder traversal. Left subtree of 1 gives 4 then 2, the right subtree gives 3, and the root 1 comes last: "4 2 3 1". "1 2 4 3" would be preorder and "2 4 1 3" inorder.

quiz.question: A trie stores N words. What is the time to check whether a word of length L is present?
quiz.explanation: search follows one child pointer per character, so it touches L nodes no matter how many words are stored. That independence from N is the point of a trie.

quiz.question: In the one-pass diameter algorithm, what does each recursive call return, and what does it record?
options: Returns 1 + max(left, right); records left + right in a global best
Returns left + right; records 1 + max(left, right)
Returns the diameter of its subtree; records nothing
Returns the number of nodes; records the depth
quiz.explanation: A parent can extend only one branch of a child’s path, so the call returns the height (one branch). The longest path that bends at the node uses both branches, left + right, which is compared against the global best.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of finding the lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a BST by walking down from the root?
options: O(n), because every node must be visited
O(h), where h is the tree height
quiz.explanation: At each node both values are either on the same side (move there) or split (stop), so you follow a single root-to-LCA path. A general binary tree needs O(n) because you cannot steer by value.
